entries.one_liner: AUC is the chance a score ranks a random good example above a random bad one; 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is a coin flip.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It is how we check a quality measure separates real transitions from broken ones before anyone picks a pass mark.
sources: Fawcett, "An Introduction to ROC Analysis", Pattern Recognition Letters 27(8), 2006
Hanley and McNeil, "The Meaning and Use of the Area under a ROC Curve", Radiology 143(1), 1982
Wikipedia, "Receiver operating characteristic" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
Take a pile of examples you already know are good or bad, and let a measure score each one.
Pick one good and one bad at random: AUC is the chance that the good one scored higher. At 1.0
the measure always ranks good above bad; at 0.5 it knows nothing, a coin flip; below 0.5 it is
upside down. The precise name is the area under the ROC (receiver operating characteristic)
curve, which plots the true-positive rate against the false-positive rate as you slide a cut-off
from strict to lenient. Its strength is that it needs no cut-off at all: it judges the ranking
first. Its limit is the flip side. It does not tell you where to put the pass mark, or how much
a false alarm costs compared with a miss; those are separate decisions made after the ranking is
shown to be good.

`apps/lyrics/vocal_presence.py` reports a held-out AUC of 0.970 for vocal coverage as an

entries.one_liner: Audio is made in blocks of frames; a block's length in milliseconds is frames divided by sample rate, and bigger blocks mean more delay.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It sets how fast a fader move or cue press reaches the speakers, and explains why ramps are counted in frames, not buffers.
sources: W3C Web Audio API specification, render quantum and AudioContext latency (baseLatency, outputLatency)
Apple Core Audio Overview, I/O buffer size, developer.apple.com
Ken C. Pohlmann, Principles of Digital Audio, 6th ed., McGraw-Hill, 2011
entries.plain:
A sound card does not take one sample at a time. The engine fills a buffer of frames (one frame
is one sample for every channel, so a stereo frame is a left and right pair) and hands the whole
block over, then starts the next. Bigger buffers are safer, because the computer has more slack
before it runs dry and glitches (an underrun, heard as a crackle), but they add delay between
your hand and your ears.

The length of a buffer is frames divided by sample rate:

ms = frames / sample_rate * 1000

At 48 kHz, 1,024 frames is 21.3 ms; at 44.1 kHz it is 23.2 ms. That is why a ramp "over one
buffer" at 1,024 frames lasts about 21 ms. Total latency is usually two or three buffers in
flight plus the device and converter delay. Under about 10 ms feels instant on a jog wheel;
past about 20 ms a scratch or cue press starts to feel late.

entries.one_liner: The audio clock counts samples and is exact; a page timer ticks about every 16 ms and wakes up late, so cuts timed from it land late.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ schedules every transport change on the audio clock and only uses page ticks to draw what was already heard.
sources: Wilson, A Tale of Two Clocks: Scheduling Web Audio with Precision, HTML5 Rocks / web.dev, 2013
Web Audio API, W3C Recommendation (AudioContext.currentTime, getOutputTimestamp, AudioWorklet render quantum), https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/
entries.plain:
A browser app has two clocks. The audio clock is driven by the sound card: it counts samples,
48,000 a second, and never wobbles. The page has timers and animation frames, which tick roughly
every 16.7 ms on a 60 Hz screen and fire whenever the main thread gets round to them, sometimes
much later if the page is busy.

If code waits for a page tick to notice "the beat has passed, cut now", the cut is late by
however far the tick was past the beat, plus the time for the message to reach the audio
thread, plus one audio block. That is 10 to 30 ms, and a DJ hears 10 ms as a flam. The fix is to
look ahead: on each tick, schedule anything due soon at its exact time on the audio clock, and
let the audio thread fire it.

entries.one_liner: A small piece of custom audio code that a web page runs on the browser's audio thread, 128 samples at a time.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ's time-stretch, level meters and dropout detector are worklets; if one misses its deadline you hear a click, so errors stop the deck rather than limp on.
sources: W3C, Web Audio API, AudioWorklet and the render quantum, https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/
MDN, AudioWorkletProcessor, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AudioWorkletProcessor
entries.plain:
A browser plays sound through a chain of built-in nodes: gains, filters, players. When you need
something the browser does not ship, such as key-locked time-stretch, you write your own node.
That code runs on a separate high-priority audio thread, not the page thread that draws the
screen, and it must hand back the next 128 samples on time, every time, a few hundred times a
second. Late means a dropout. It talks to the page only by passing messages, so it never waits
on the screen.

The precise terms: an `AudioWorkletProcessor` registered with `registerProcessor`, called once
per render quantum of 128 frames by the Web Audio rendering thread.

entries.one_liner: Which beat of the bar a moment sits on, 1 to 4; two decks can share every beat and still disagree about which one is the 1.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Beat sync in BAR mode refuses to lock two decks unless their bar phases agree, so drops and phrase changes land together.
sources: Pioneer DJ CDJ-3000 Operating Instructions (Beat Sync, bar and phrase display), AlphaTheta
Butler, Unlocking the Groove: Rhythm, Meter, and Musical Design in Electronic Dance Music, Indiana University Press, 2006
entries.plain:
Dance music counts in fours, and the "1" matters: that is where the drop hits, where the
bassline restarts, where a new 8, 16 or 32 bar phrase begins. Bar phase is simply "which count
are we on right now". Two decks can be perfectly beatmatched, every kick landing together, while
one deck is on its 1 and the other is on its 4. It sounds fine for a while, then the second
track's drop arrives a beat early and the whole mix feels like it tripped.

Precisely: bar phase is the beat index modulo the bar length (4 here), counted from the nearest
preceding downbeat. Beat phase is the fraction of the way through the current beat. Sync needs
both.

entries.one_liner: The moment in a blend where the outgoing track's bass is cut and the incoming track's bass comes in, on one downbeat.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Two basslines at once sound muddy and can overload a club system, so where and how sharply the swap lands decides whether a blend sounds clean.
sources: Spotify Support, Mixed playlists, https://support.spotify.com/us/article/mixed-playlists/
Wikipedia, Beatmatching, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beatmatching
entries.plain:
In a long blend you bring the new track in with its low EQ turned down, so only its highs and
mids join. Then, on a downbeat, you turn the old track's lows down and the new track's lows up at
the same time. That is the bass swap. Done on the bar line, the groove passes from one kick and
bassline to the other without a bar of mud or a bar of nothing.

Where it falls is a choice. A center swap lands at the mix point, in the middle of the blend, so
the new track owns the floor for the second half. An end swap holds the old bass until the blend
finishes, so the old track keeps the weight longer. Reviewers report Spotify's EQ lane offering
both, as Center bass and End bass swap.

entries.one_liner: Beam search keeps the k best partial answers at every step instead of committing to the single best one, like greedy does.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It is how PLAY IT orders a set today, with a beam of 8 partial orders, and it explains both why that beats greedy and where it still falls short.
sources: Russell and Norvig, Artificial Intelligence, A Modern Approach, 4th ed., Pearson, 2020 (local beam search)
Lowerre, The HARPY Speech Recognition System, PhD thesis, Carnegie Mellon University, 1976
Wikipedia, "Beam search" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
Greedy ordering picks the best next track and never looks back. That is fast, but the best first
move can lead into a corner: a lovely transition now that leaves only rough ones later. Beam
search keeps several partial answers alive. At each step it extends every kept partial order by
every remaining track, scores them, keeps the top k (the beam width) and drops the rest. With a
width of 1 it is greedy; with an unlimited width it is a full search that tries everything. A
width of a handful is the cheap middle: a route that looks slightly worse early can survive long
enough to win. Its limits are that a pruned route never comes back, and that by the end all the
kept routes often share the same opening, so a bad early choice can still be locked in. It
builds forward only and does not go back to polish what it already placed.

entries.in_open_dj:
`apps/dj_copilot/solver.py` is the "greedy beam PLAY IT solver": `suggest_order` runs a beam of
width 8 by default, scoring each candidate next track with key 0.35, BPM 0.35, energy 0.25 and
artist 0.05 against the set goal's energy arc, and pruning by the summed score with a fixed tie-break, so the same
inputs always give the same order. Pinned openers, peaks and closers are
honored. The playlist-ordering research (Tue 27 Oct 2026) keeps this beam as the baseline and
plans a local-search pass after it, because the beam has no improvement step and tends to leave
the roughest transitions at the end of the set.

entries.one_liner: A list of timestamps saying where every beat of a track falls, which beats start a bar, and the tempo between them.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Sync, quantize, beat loops, beat jumps and bar-aligned mixes all read the grid, so a wrong grid breaks every one of them at once.
sources: rekordbox Operating Instructions (beat grid editing), AlphaTheta / Pioneer DJ
Foscarin, Schluter, Widmer, Beat This! Accurate Beat Tracking Without DBN Postprocessing, ISMIR 2024
Beatmatching, Wikipedia (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
A beat grid is the ruler laid over a track. Each mark says "a beat happens here", and every
fourth mark is a downbeat, the first beat of a bar. Software reads the gaps between marks to get
the tempo, so a track that speeds up gets marks that slowly creep closer together. With a good
grid the computer knows the music's time as well as you do; with a bad one it confidently lines
things up in the wrong place.

The precise version: a grid file is an ordered list of beats, each holding a time in seconds (or
milliseconds), a beat number 1 to 4 inside its bar, and the local tempo. A fixed-tempo track can
be stored as one anchor plus a BPM; a "dynamic" grid stores every beat.
entries.in_open_dj:
Two sources feed the deck. The rekordbox grid comes from the track's ANLZ file (the PQTZ tag,
read with pyrekordbox) and reaches the page as the beat list in
`apps/webui/frontend/src/lib/rb/anlz-types.ts`. Our own grid is built in `apps/analysis_beatgrid`:
`beat_this_runner.py` finds beats and downbeats, `grid_fit.py` and `tempo_map.py` fit them into
a clean grid, and `grid_quality.py` flags grids that look suspect so sync can treat them with
care. A DJ sees the grid as the tick marks on the waveform.

entries.one_liner: An EQ band that boosts or cuts a hill of frequencies around one center point and leaves both ends of the spectrum alone.
entries.why_it_matters_here: The MID knob on every Open DJ deck is a bell at 1.2 kHz, so it shapes vocals and leads but can never silence them.
sources: Robert Bristow-Johnson, "Audio EQ Cookbook" (peakingEQ), W3C note, https://www.w3.org/TR/audio-eq-cookbook/
W3C, "Web Audio API", BiquadFilterNode type "peaking", https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/
Bob Katz, "Mastering Audio: The Art and the Science", Focal Press, 2015 (chapter on equalization)
entries.plain:
A bell EQ raises or lowers a band of frequencies around a center point. Plot what it does and you
get a hill (boost) or a valley (cut) shaped like a bell, which is where the name comes from. Below
and above the bell the sound is untouched.

It has three settings. Frequency says where the center sits. Gain says how high or deep the bell
goes, in dB. Q says how wide it is: a low Q is a broad gentle hump, a high Q a narrow spike. On a
studio parametric EQ you get all three knobs; on a DJ mixer the mid knob is usually a bell with
the frequency and Q fixed, so only gain is yours.

The precise name is peaking EQ. Because the skirts of the bell always fade back to 0 dB, even a
very deep cut leaves the edges of the band in place: a bell can carve, but it cannot kill a band.
entries.in_open_dj:
The deck MID band is a peaking biquad at 1.2 kHz with Q = 1, gain from -26 dB at the bottom of
the knob to +6 dB at the top (`EQ_FREQ_MID_HZ`, `EQ_MID_Q`, `EQ_MIN_DB`, `EQ_MAX_DB` in
`apps/audio-engine/src/mixer.rs`; coefficients in `apps/audio-engine/src/dsp.rs`, which has a test
that the bell reaches its gain exactly at the center). The browser engine uses Web Audio's
`peaking` node with the same numbers.

entries.one_liner: A filter tuned so every frequency it passes is delayed by the same amount, keeping drum hits sharp at the price of a soft, slow roll-off.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It is one of two common shapes for isolator crossovers, picked when keeping the kick transient intact matters more than a steep split.
sources: W. E. Thomson, "Delay networks having maximally flat frequency characteristics", Proceedings of the IEE, Part III, 96(44), 1949
Julius O. Smith III, "Introduction to Digital Filters with Audio Applications", CCRMA Stanford, https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/filters/
Wikipedia, "Bessel filter" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
Every filter delays sound a little. Most filters delay frequencies near their cutoff more than the
rest, so a sharp attack, made of many frequencies at once, comes out with its parts slightly out
of step: it overshoots and rings. A Bessel filter is designed the other way round. It keeps the
delay as even as possible across the passband (maximally flat group delay), so a kick or a snare
keeps its shape and does not ring.

The price is the magnitude response. A Bessel filter bends over gently and slowly near the
cutoff, so for the same order it separates bands less sharply than a Butterworth, and you need a
higher order to get the same isolation.

It still costs time: an even delay is still a delay. For a 4th-order Bessel low-pass with its
-3 dB point at 100 Hz, every passband frequency arrives about 3 ms late. Higher order and lower
cutoff both make it longer.

entries.one_liner: A tiny five-number filter recipe that nearly every digital EQ band, shelf and sweep filter is built from.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Every EQ band and both sides of the filter knob on an Open DJ deck are one biquad each, run the same way in the browser and the native engine.
sources: Robert Bristow-Johnson, "Audio EQ Cookbook", W3C Audio Working Group note, https://www.w3.org/TR/audio-eq-cookbook/
W3C, "Web Audio API", BiquadFilterNode section, https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/
Julius O. Smith III, "Introduction to Digital Filters with Audio Applications", CCRMA Stanford, https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/filters/
entries.plain:
A biquad is a very small filter. For every new sample it looks at that sample, the two samples
before it and its own two previous outputs, multiplies each by a fixed number and adds them up.
Those five numbers (the coefficients) decide what it does: the same little machine becomes a
low-pass, a high-pass, a bell, a shelf or a notch just by swapping them.

That is why DSP builds almost everything from biquads. One block is cheap, well understood and
stays numerically stable, and a steeper filter is simply several biquads in a row, called a
cascade of second-order sections. "Biquad" is short for biquadratic: its transfer function is one
quadratic divided by another. The recipe itself is the point:

y[n] = b0 x[n] + b1 x[n-1] + b2 x[n-2] - a1 y[n-1] - a2 y[n-2]

`apps/audio-engine/src/dsp.rs` computes biquad coefficients in exactly the forms the Web Audio

entries.one_liner: Bradley-Terry turns many "A or B?" picks into one strength per item, so blind pairwise votes become a scale.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It is the planned way to turn the founder's blind A/B picks between transitions into weights for the quality measure.
sources: Bradley and Terry, "Rank Analysis of Incomplete Block Designs I. The Method of Paired Comparisons", Biometrika 39(3/4), 1952
Hunter, "MM Algorithms for Generalized Bradley-Terry Models", Annals of Statistics 32(1), 2004
Agresti, Categorical Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Wiley, 2013 (chapter on paired comparisons)
entries.plain:
Ask a DJ to rate a transition out of 10 and the answer drifts with mood, with the previous
track, with what "7" means today. Ask "A or B?" and the answer is far more stable. The
Bradley-Terry model turns a pile of those pairwise picks into one number per item, a strength,
chosen so the predicted chance that A beats B matches the picks as closely as possible:

    P(A beats B) = 1 / (1 + exp(-(b_A - b_B)))

It suits blind A/B ratings for three reasons. A comparison needs no shared anchor. Not every
pair has to be heard, because strengths link through chains (A beat B, B beat C). And the fit
reports its own uncertainty. The useful extension: make each strength a weighted sum of measured
features of the transition, and fitting the picks yields the weights, which is how ratings
calibrate a measure.

entries.one_liner: The filter shape with the flattest possible passband: no bumps, no ripple, then a smooth bend down through -3 dB at the cutoff.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It is the default low-pass and high-pass shape in audio, used in Open DJ's waveform split and approximated by the deck filter knob.
sources: Stephen Butterworth, "On the Theory of Filter Amplifiers", Experimental Wireless and the Wireless Engineer 7, 1930
Robert Bristow-Johnson, "Audio EQ Cookbook" (LPF and HPF with Q = 1 divided by root 2), W3C note, https://www.w3.org/TR/audio-eq-cookbook/
Wikipedia, "Butterworth filter" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
Stephen Butterworth's 1930 design asks for one thing: the part of the sound the filter keeps
should come through as flat as mathematically possible. No hump before the cutoff, no ripple, just
level, then a smooth bend down. Every Butterworth filter, whatever its order, is exactly 3 dB down
at its cutoff, and beyond it falls at 6 dB per octave for each order.

That makes it the sensible default whenever a filter should be heard as "less of the top" or
"less of the bottom" and nothing else. Its compromise sits in the middle of the alternatives: it
cuts more sharply near the cutoff than a Bessel filter but overshoots a little on drum hits,
more as the order rises, and it has none of the passband ripple steeper designs accept.

A 2nd-order Butterworth is one biquad with Q = 0.707 (1 divided by the square root of 2).

entries.one_liner: Pick the measurable number that best agrees with a person's blind ratings, then lock it in as the bar.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It is how a subjective "this blend feels smooth" becomes a number Open DJ can test and ratchet every round.
sources: Thurstone, "A Law of Comparative Judgment", Psychological Review 34(4), 1927
ITU-R BS.1534, Method for the subjective assessment of intermediate quality level of audio (MUSHRA), 2015
Wikipedia, "Criterion validity" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
Much of what makes a transition "good" is taste. A computer cannot measure feel directly, so we
pick a measurable proxy, a number computed from the audio, and check it against a person's
blind ratings: they listen without knowing which variant is which, they rate or pick, and we see
which proxy agrees with them most. The winner goes into the spec as a pass mark and a regression
metric. Calibration is only for the taste layer. Hygiene, meaning objective correctness (no
clipping, no NaN, beats aligned within a few milliseconds, a null test that cancels), needs no
ratings: it is right or wrong. Spending a person's ears on hygiene wastes the scarcest resource
we have, so ratings go only to the judgements that are still uncertain, and the proxy is later
checked on ratings it was not fitted to.

entries.one_liner: A clock of 24 keys: numbers 1 to 12 around, A for minor and B for major. One step around or straight across mixes cleanly.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ reads every key as a wheel position, so the wheel decides which tracks the suggester offers and how a key match is scored.

entries.plain:
The Camelot wheel is a cheat sheet that turns music theory into numbers. Twelve numbers sit
around a clock face, and each number holds two keys: a minor key on the inner ring (A) and a
major key on the outer ring (B). "Adjacent" means one step around the clock on the same letter
(8A to 7A or 9A) or straight across on the same number (8A to 8B). Each of those moves changes at
most one note of the scale, so two tracks overlap without sour notes.

The precise term: the wheel is the circle of fifths relabeled, so each step clockwise is up a
perfect fifth. Traktor uses the same idea under the name Open Key, with m for minor and d for
major, rotated so that C major is 1d where Camelot calls it 8B. Converting is a fixed offset:
the Open Key number is the Camelot number minus 7, wrapping around 12 (8A is 1m, 1B is 6d).

It says three things. First, a good transition is a plan, not a fade: five decisions per pair
(where to leave the outgoing track, where to enter the incoming one, how many bars overlap, what
moves during the overlap, what happens to tempo). Second, a ladder of six rungs from AutoPlay to
AutoDJ: rung 0 starts the next track; 1 is a timed crossfade; 2 a structure-aware beatmatched
blend with gain matching; 3 a styled transition chosen per pair (bass swap, filter, echo out,
riser, stem swap, cut); 4 re-arranges the tracks (loops, extended parts, big tempo gaps); 5 is
intent-driven, a prompt drives selection and every transition and the set adapts live. Spotify
sits on 2 and 3; Open DJ's AutoPlay is rung 1. Third, the split: an LLM plans, a deterministic
executor performs the plan sample-accurately, and an offline render scores it before it goes
live. The plan is a `TransitionPlan` in absolute bars with a named style, parameters, and a
`trim_db` per deck, the gain offset in dB that matches the incoming track's loudness to the
outgoing one. "The canon's trim_db" in the brief means that field.

entries.one_liner: A cent is a hundredth of a semitone, the unit for pitch changes too small to call a note, like the drift a tempo nudge causes.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Tempo trims and fader moves without key lock shift pitch by cents, which decides when a stretcher is worth engaging at all.
sources: Ellis, On the Musical Scales of Various Nations, Journal of the Society of Arts, 1885 (origin of the cent)
Cent (music), Wikipedia (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
A semitone is one piano key. A cent is one hundredth of that, so an octave is 1200 cents.
Cents matter in DJing because tempo and pitch are tied together when key lock is off: speed a
track up by 1 percent and it goes up about 17 cents. A careful listener notices a change of
roughly 5 cents in a held tone; a change of 1 cent is far below what anyone hears in a club.

That is why a 1 cent threshold is a sensible switch for a stretcher. If the tempo ratio is within
1 cent of exactly 1.0, playing the audio straight (varispeed) shifts pitch by less than anyone
can hear, so the deck can skip the stretcher and avoid its latency, CPU and artifacts. Past
that, key lock needs the stretcher. The formula: cents = 1200 x log2(ratio), and 1 cent is a
ratio of 1.000578, about 0.058 percent.
entries.in_open_dj:
Not yet as a threshold: the code has no 1 cent switch. The Rust engine
(`apps/audio-engine/src/stretch.rs`) decides on the setting instead: Master Tempo off with no key
shift means no stretcher, and otherwise the stretcher always runs, even at unity, where the
quality table measures it. A cent-based bypass would belong there and in
`apps/webui/frontend/src/lib/rb/stretch-adapter.ts`. The phase lock's 0.3 percent trim cap is
about 5 cents.

entries.one_liner: Twelve numbers per moment, one per note name C to B, saying how much of each note is sounding. Key detection reads it.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ's own key detector computes chroma for the whole track and matches it against 24 key templates.
sources: Mueller, Fundamentals of Music Processing, Springer, 2nd ed. 2021, chroma features
Krumhansl, Cognitive Foundations of Musical Pitch, Oxford University Press, 1990
librosa documentation, feature.chroma_cqt, https://librosa.org/doc/
Wikipedia, Chroma feature (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
Chroma throws away which octave a note is in and keeps only its name. A low A on the bassline,
a middle A on the pads and a high A in the vocal all pour into the same bucket. The result is
twelve buckets, C through B, measured again every few tens of milliseconds. Plot them over time
and you get a chromagram: a 12-row picture of the harmony with the drums mostly washed out.

Key detection works by averaging chroma across the track and asking which key's "shape" it
resembles. Each key has a template of how often its notes tend to appear (the home note and the
fifth strongest, notes outside the scale weakest); the standard ones come from Krumhansl's
listening experiments. Rotate the major and minor templates to all twelve home notes, correlate
each of the 24 with the track's profile, and the best correlation wins. The size of that win is
the key confidence.

entries.one_liner: A 3-band EQ splits the spectrum at two crossover points, by convention near 250 Hz and 2.5 kHz, into low, mid and high.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Where the split sits decides what a bass swap removes and what the colored waveform paints as bass, mids and highs.
sources: Siegfried Linkwitz, "Active Crossover Networks for Noncoincident Drivers", Journal of the Audio Engineering Society 24(1), 1976
Rane Corporation, "Linkwitz-Riley Crossovers: A Primer" (RaneNote 160), https://www.ranecommercial.com/
Wikipedia, "Audio crossover" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
A crossover is a pair of filters that hand the sound over from one band to the next: below the
crossover frequency the lower band takes it, above it the upper band does, and around the point
they overlap. Two crossovers make three bands.

DJ software commonly puts them near 250 Hz and 2.5 kHz. Below 250 Hz sit the kick's thump and the
bassline. Between 250 Hz and 2.5 kHz sit most of the vocal, the snare body, chords and leads.
Above 2.5 kHz sit hi-hats, cymbals, consonants and air. These are conventions, not laws: mixer
makers move them, and a kick's click lives up in the highs while a vocal's warmth reaches below
250 Hz, so no split separates instruments perfectly.

Why is the mid band's center about 791 Hz and not halfway? Three bands need exactly two split
points, low/mid at 250 Hz and mid/high at 2,500 Hz. Halfway in hertz would be 1,375 Hz, but
hearing and musical pitch work in ratios: each octave doubles the frequency. Halfway in octaves
is the geometric mean, sqrt(250 x 2500) = 791 Hz, which sits the same ratio (about 3.2 times,
or 1.66 octaves) above 250 Hz as it sits below 2,500 Hz.

A good crossover gives back the original when the bands are added up at equal gain. The usual
choice, the Linkwitz-Riley crossover, crosses each pair at -6 dB so the sum is flat.
entries.in_open_dj:
Two different splits exist. The deck EQ is not a crossover: it is a 250 Hz low shelf, a 1.2 kHz
bell and a 5 kHz high shelf (`apps/audio-engine/src/mixer.rs`), so its "bands" overlap broadly.
The three-band colored waveform is a true split at 200 Hz and 4 kHz
(`apps/audio-engine/src/waveform.rs`, `apps/analysis_waveform/decode.py`), chosen to resemble
rekordbox's display; the decode module says the numbers were stated, not discovered.

entries.one_liner: The frequency where a filter has turned the sound down by 3 dB, the line between what it keeps and what it removes.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Turning Open DJ's filter knob moves the cutoff, sweeping it from 20 kHz down to 130 Hz on the low-pass side.
sources: Julius O. Smith III, "Introduction to Digital Filters with Audio Applications", CCRMA Stanford, https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/filters/
W3C, "Web Audio API", BiquadFilterNode frequency attribute, https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/
Wikipedia, "Cutoff frequency" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
A low-pass filter keeps the lows and removes the highs, but there is no hard wall between them.
The cutoff frequency is the agreed marker: the point where the filter has turned the signal down
by 3 dB. That is half the power, or about 71 percent of the amplitude, a step quiet enough to
notice but far from silent.

Below the cutoff (for a low-pass) is the passband, kept almost unchanged. Above it the sound
fades away at the filter's slope, so content just past the cutoff is still clearly there, only
quieter. A high-pass is the mirror image. When a DJ turns a filter knob, what moves is the cutoff;
how fast the sound disappears beyond it is the order, and any bump right at it is the resonance.

One wrinkle: on a resonant filter the response near the cutoff is lifted, so the true -3 dB point
moves away from the number on the dial. Engineers then say "corner" or "center" frequency instead.
entries.in_open_dj:
The filter knob maps position to cutoff exponentially in Hz, which is even steps in octaves:
the low-pass side sweeps 20 kHz down to 130 Hz, the high-pass side 30 Hz up to 6.3 kHz, with a
2 percent dead zone at the center (`FILTER_*` in `apps/audio-engine/src/mixer.rs`,
`filterParamsFromKnob` in `apps/webui/frontend/src/lib/rb/audio-engine-guards.ts`). Because Web
Audio reads Q in dB, the dial value is a corner with slight lift, not an exact -3 dB point.

entries.one_liner: dBFS measures a digital level against the loudest value the system can store; 0 dBFS is the ceiling and every real signal reads below it.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Every meter, clip light and gain knob in Open DJ is expressed in dBFS, so it is the shared ruler for the whole mixer.
sources: AES17-2020, AES standard method for digital audio engineering, measurement of digital audio equipment (definition of full scale)
IEC 60268-10, Peak programme level meters
Wikipedia: dBFS, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DBFS (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
A digital audio file stores each sample as a number with a hard top: the biggest value the
format can hold. dBFS ("decibels relative to full scale") says how far a level sits below that
top. 0 dBFS is the ceiling itself, so every useful reading is negative: -6 dBFS is half the
maximum amplitude, -20 dBFS is one tenth. Nothing can be louder than 0 dBFS inside a fixed-point
file; anything that tries is cut off flat, which is clipping.

The decibel is a ratio, so the same rule works everywhere: each -6 dB halves the amplitude, and
each -20 dB divides it by ten.

dB = 20 * log10(amplitude / full_scale)

entries.in_open_dj:
The channel and master meters work in dBFS: `apps/webui/frontend/src/lib/rb/meter-math.ts`
sets the scale floor at -60 dBFS (`METER_FLOOR_DBFS`) and the latched clip light at -0.1 dBFS
(`CLIP_DBFS`), with segments spaced in dB rather than in raw amplitude so the bottom of the bar
still moves for real music. The offline scanner in `apps/loudness/scan.py` reports true peak
in dBTP alongside the loudness figure. Internally the mixer computes in
floating point, which can briefly exceed 1.0; the ceiling bites where audio is written to a
fixed-point file, as in the recorder and WAV writer in `apps/audio-engine/src/`, which clamp to
the range -1 to 1.

entries.one_liner: The thin native app that gives a web interface its own window, icon and file picker, while the real work happens in a separate engine.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ keeps the shell thin so the app behaves the same in its own window or a browser tab, and so the shell can change without touching the mixer.
sources: Tauri 2 documentation, https://v2.tauri.app/
Electron documentation, Process Model, https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/tutorial/process-model
entries.plain:
Open DJ's screens are a web page. A desktop shell wraps that page in a normal Mac or Windows app:
a window, a dock icon, a quit menu, an updater, a native folder picker. Tauri does this with the
system's own web view and a small Rust program; Electron does it by bundling its own copy of
Chromium. Either way the shell should stay a window, not an application. The engine process
owns the library, the analysis, the state and the audio decisions.

The split matters for a DJ because a crash or update in one half should not take the other half
down with it, and because anything the shell owns is something a browser tab or an agent cannot
reach.

entries.one_liner: The DJ sends the outgoing track into an echo, cuts the track, and lets the fading repeats fill the gap while the next track comes in.
entries.why_it_matters_here: The echo_out transition style depends on it, and the tail only sounds smooth if feedback is ramped, never jumped, and the effect sits after the fader.
sources: Mixxx 2.5 manual, Effects chapter, https://manual.mixxx.org/2.5/en/chapters/effects
Mixxx 2.5 manual, Glossary, https://manual.mixxx.org/2.5/en/glossary
Udo Zoelzer (ed.), DAFX Digital Audio Effects, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2011 (delay with feedback)
entries.plain:
An echo out is a way to leave a track without a long blend. Just before the mix point the DJ
turns on an echo (a delay with feedback) on the outgoing deck, then cuts the track: fader down,
or a kill. The track stops feeding the echo, but the echo keeps playing the last beat back, each
repeat quieter than the one before, so the room hears a fading tail instead of a hole while the
next track comes in underneath.

Feedback sets how many repeats there are and how long the tail lasts. A common move is to ramp
feedback up as the fader comes down, say from 30 to 70 percent, so the tail grows longer and
smoother exactly when the dry track disappears. The ramp has to be smooth: jumping the value in
one step can click, and pushing it too high builds into a runaway wash. That is what "feedback
ramping fixes" in Mixxx notes are about: the effect moves from the old value to the new one over
a buffer instead of jumping. The echo must also sit after the fader; Mixxx's manual says its
effects are processed after the deck faders so an echo keeps sounding once its input is cut.
entries.in_open_dj:
Not yet. The echo_out transition style is listed in the transition plan but not built; it is
proposed, not on main, and there is no echo effect on main either. It would belong in the effects
module of the Web Audio engine under `apps/webui/frontend/src/lib/` and in the Rust engine under
`apps/audio-engine/src/`, and the Effects lane of the transition plan would carry the send and
feedback ramp alongside the fader lane.

entries.one_liner: Delay repeats the sound; echo is a delay with fading, beat-locked repeats; reverb smears it into a room-like wash with no distinct repeats.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Each leaves a different tail when the track stops, so each hides a different kind of bad transition.
sources: Udo Zoelzer (ed.), DAFX Digital Audio Effects, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2011
AlphaTheta, DJM-900NXS2 Operating Instructions (Beat FX ECHO, DELAY, REVERB), https://www.pioneerdj.com/
entries.plain:
All three add sound after the original, but the shape of the tail differs. A delay plays clear
copies at a set time; with little feedback it might be one or two slaps. An echo on a DJ mixer
is a delay tuned for leaving: beat-locked repeats that fade away over a bar or two, so you can
stop a track and its rhythm keeps ticking out. Reverb has no separate repeats at all. It is
thousands of tiny reflections blended into a wash, like singing in a hall, and it hides rhythm
rather than repeating it.

In a mix, echo out exits a track cleanly on the beat, reverb wash covers a tempo or key mismatch
by blurring it, and a short delay adds groove without leaving.

entries.one_liner: Jump two numbers up the Camelot wheel, a whole tone higher, to lift the room. Best as a quick, phrase-aligned cut, not a long blend.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ has energy boost and energy drop as named key moves, off by default because they are a choice, not a safe match.
sources: Mixed In Key, Use Advanced Harmonic Mixing Techniques, https://mixedinkey.com/Book/Use-Advanced-Harmonic-Mixing-Techniques/
DJ.Studio, How To DJ using compatible Keys, https://dj.studio/blog/compatible-keys
Wikipedia, Modulation (music) (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
An energy boost mix moves two numbers clockwise on the same letter, 8A to 10A or 8B to 10B.
Because each wheel step is a fifth, two steps land exactly one whole tone (two semitones) above
where you started: C major becomes D major. Everything the crowd was humming suddenly sits
higher, and the ear reads that as a lift, the same trick pop songs use in their last chorus.

The catch is that the two keys share only five of seven notes. Overlapping them for a long
blend lets the two odd notes rub. So DJs use it as a short move: mix the drums of the incoming
track early, keep its melody out with EQ, then cut cleanly on a phrase start (a drop or a new
16-bar section) so the key change arrives as an event rather than a smear. The reverse move, two
numbers counterclockwise, is an energy drop and works the same way to cool a floor down.

entries.one_liner: An equal-power crossfade uses cosine and sine gains so the mix holds steady loudness, each side at -3 dB in the middle, with no dip.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ's crossfader uses this law, so a slow blend through the center keeps the room level instead of sagging.
sources: Julius O. Smith III, Physical Audio Signal Processing, CCRMA Stanford (online book), panning and power laws
Pioneer DJ DJM-900NXS2 operating instructions, crossfader curve selector
Wikipedia: Panning (audio), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panning_(audio) (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
A crossfader decides how much of deck A and deck B you hear at each position. The obvious design
is linear: at the center each deck gets half its amplitude. But half amplitude is -6 dB, and two
different tracks (uncorrelated material) add by power, not by amplitude, so the middle of a
linear fade comes out about 3 dB quieter than either end. The room hears a sag.

Equal power fixes that by using a quarter of a circle. At position x from 0 to 1:

gain_A = cos(x * pi/2)    gain_B = sin(x * pi/2)

Because cos squared plus sin squared is always 1, total power stays constant. At the center
both gains are 0.707 (one over the square root of two), which is -3 dB each, and the two powers
add back to 0 dB. The catch is correlated material: if both decks play the same kick in phase,
amplitudes add, and the center reads about +3 dB instead.
entries.in_open_dj:
`apps/audio-engine/src/mixer.rs` defines `xf_gain`: a channel assigned to A gets
`cos(x * pi/2)`, one assigned to B gets `cos((1 - x) * pi/2)` (the same as the sine), and THRU
ignores the crossfader. A unit test there, `crossfader_is_equal_power`, pins the law. The
headphone cue and master blend in `apps/webui/frontend/src/lib/player/headphones.ts` uses the
same equal-power shape. I did not find a selectable sharp "cut" curve for scratch mixing.

entries.one_liner: Prove a measure against outside evidence, such as real DJs' mixes and published studies, before spending anyone's ears on it.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It keeps the transition score from encoding one person's taste and saves the founder's listening time for the questions only he can answer.
sources: Cronbach and Meehl, "Construct Validity in Psychological Tests", Psychological Bulletin 52(4), 1955
Steyerberg, Clinical Prediction Models, 2nd ed., Springer, 2019 (internal versus external validation)
Wikipedia, "External validity" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
A measure tuned on one person's ratings may end up measuring that person. And a person's
listening time is the scarcest thing the project has. External validation tests a measure
against evidence from outside the team first. Real-world positives are transitions real DJs
chose to play and publish, assumed to be mostly fine; damage copies of them on purpose (one beat
late, one bar late, a random bar) and the measure must tell the real ones from the broken ones.
Published studies and labeled datasets add more: if a study reports how often DJs mix at phrase
boundaries, a measure that is right should reproduce that share. If a measure cannot tell a real
DJ's mix from the same mix shifted one beat, no amount of taste tuning will rescue it. Human
spot checks come last, aimed only where the measure and the outside evidence disagree.

`apps/lyrics/vocal_presence.py` is the worked example: its score was first validated on
MTG-Jamendo tracks with unanimous three-annotator voice labels (held-out AUC 0.970), and only
then was its threshold set from the founder's blind ratings. The proposed quality-measure plan
(not yet on main) plans the same order for transitions: real-DJ
discrimination on a 500-transition sample, reproduction of published DJ-mix findings, and
mutation tests, with an evidence ledger marking each claim validated-external, validated by the
founder, rejected or needing a recheck.

entries.one_liner: Feedback sets how much of each echo is fed back to echo again, so repeats fade slowly or fast; ping-pong bounces them left and right.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Feedback decides how long an echo out covers the gap between tracks; too much and it piles up into a wash that fights the incoming track.
sources: Udo Zoelzer (ed.), DAFX Digital Audio Effects, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2011 (delay with feedback)
Wikipedia, Delay (audio effect), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delay_(audio_effect)
entries.plain:
A delay plays the sound back a moment later. Feedback sends some of that delayed copy back into
the delay, so it repeats again, and again, each time quieter. At 50 percent feedback each repeat
is half as loud as the one before; at 90 percent the repeats hang around for a long time; at 100
or more they never die and build up. For DJ use the delay time is locked to the beat, so repeats
land on 1/2, 3/4 or 1 beat and stay musical.

Ping-pong routes the repeats so they alternate between the left and right speakers. It sounds
wider and moves, but on a mono club system the bounce collapses back to one place.

entries.one_liner: One step on the Camelot wheel is a perfect fifth up or a fourth down, and the two keys differ by a single note.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ's default key filter offers one step either way on the wheel, and scores it just under a same-key match.
sources: Mixed In Key, Harmonic Mixing book, https://mixedinkey.com/Book/
Mueller, Fundamentals of Music Processing, Springer, 2nd ed. 2021
Wikipedia, Circle of fifths (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
A fifth is the interval from C up to G: seven semitones, the "power chord" sound. Its two notes
vibrate in a simple 3 to 2 ratio, so they blend almost like one note. A fourth is the same pair
upside down (G up to C, five semitones). Going up a fifth and going down a fourth land on the
same note name, which is why +1 on the wheel covers both.

Keys a fifth apart share six of their seven notes. C major and G major differ only in F versus
F#. When you mix 8B into 9B, every chord in one track still finds most of its notes in the other,
and the one note that moves only moves a semitone. That is why +1 and -1 sound right: the
change is audible as a lift (clockwise) or a settling (counterclockwise), never as a clash.

The wheel is built from this: walk clockwise twelve fifths and you visit every key once before
returning home. So wheel steps count fifths, not piano keys.

The `adjacent` rule in `CAMELOT_RULES` (`apps/shared/harmonic.py`) allows one step either way on

fifths up is one semitone up.

entries.one_liner: A filter's order counts its stages; each one adds 6 dB per octave of slope, so higher order means a steeper, sharper cut.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ's filter knob is a 12 dB per octave biquad and its waveform split is 24 dB per octave, and the difference is audible.
sources: Julius O. Smith III, "Introduction to Digital Filters with Audio Applications", CCRMA Stanford, https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/filters/
Richard G. Lyons, "Understanding Digital Signal Processing", 3rd edition, Prentice Hall, 2010
Wikipedia, "Roll-off" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
Past its cutoff, a filter does not stop sound dead. It turns it down more and more the further you
go, and the rate is the slope, measured in dB per octave (an octave is a doubling of frequency, say
1 kHz to 2 kHz). The order is how many basic stages, or poles, the filter has, and each adds
6 dB per octave.

So a 1st-order filter is a gentle tilt, a 2nd-order (one biquad) falls 12 dB per octave, and a
4th-order (two biquads in a row) falls 24 dB per octave, which is the classic steep sound of DJ
filters and isolator crossovers. 48 dB per octave is close to a wall.

Steeper is not free. Each extra order adds more phase shift and more delay near the cutoff, more
ringing on drum hits, and more computation. A 24 dB slope sounds tighter on a sweep; a 12 dB slope
sounds smoother and more open.

entries.one_liner: Send a reviewer who has seen none of the discussion, only the goal and the material, and ask what the team missed.
entries.why_it_matters_here: The people and agents who built a measure share its blind spots, so Open DJ schedules unprimed reviewers to find them.
sources: Fagan, "Design and Code Inspections to Reduce Errors in Program Development", IBM Systems Journal 15(3), 1976
Klein, "Performing a Project Premortem", Harvard Business Review, September 2007
Wikipedia, "Red team" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
The people who built something share its assumptions, and an assumption everyone shares is
invisible to all of them. A fresh-eyes review sends someone who has seen none of the discussion,
a new person or a new agent, with only the goal and where to find the material, and asks what is
missing or wrong. "Unprimed" is the important word. Hand the reviewer your hypothesis, your
reasoning or your worries and it will tend to check exactly those and agree, which feels like
confirmation but is only an echo. Keep the brief short, let it look anywhere, and write down
what it finds whether or not the team adopts it, so a later reader can see what was raised and
why it was set aside. It is cheap, so it is worth doing on a schedule rather than only when
something already feels off.

entries.one_liner: An EQ whose band, turned fully down, removes that band completely; it needs an isolator, because a shelf only ever turns a band down by a fixed amount.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ's LOW knob at zero still leaks bass, so a two-bassline swap is less clean than on a full-kill mixer.
sources: Allen and Heath, "Xone:92 User Guide" (EQ total kill), https://www.allen-heath.com/
Pioneer DJ, "DJM-900NXS2 Operating Instructions" (EQ curve ISOLATOR and EQ settings), https://www.pioneerdj.com/
Robert Bristow-Johnson, "Audio EQ Cookbook" (shelf gain and slope), W3C note, https://www.w3.org/TR/audio-eq-cookbook/
entries.plain:
On a full-kill mixer, turning the bass knob all the way down makes the bass disappear: the band
goes to silence, minus infinity in dB. Many mixers also have kill buttons that do this in one
press. DJs lean on it for the bass swap, where one track's bass is removed exactly as the other's
comes in, so two basslines never fight.

A shelving EQ cannot do this, for two reasons. Its depth is a fixed gain, often -26 dB, so the
bass is much quieter but still present. And its ramp from cut to flat has a fixed gentle slope:
making the cut deeper does not make the ramp steeper, it only drags the ramp further into the
mids, so at the corner frequency you get roughly half the cut and the low mids suffer as well.

So a kill is "not a deeper shelf". A shelf lowers everything below its corner by a fixed amount
and stops there; Open DJ's low shelf bottoms out at -26 dB. Pushing that shelf to -60 dB would
still be a shelf. A kill is a different filter, an isolator, which keeps attenuating toward zero
below the crossover, so nothing is left to leak.

A full kill needs an isolator: crossover filters split the bass off as its own band, and that band
is turned down to zero on its own. Some DJ software combines both, keeping shelves for the upper
part of the knob and fading an isolator band to zero at the bottom.

entries.one_liner: A gain ramp glides a volume change over a few milliseconds instead of jumping, which stops the clicks and buzz called zipper noise.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Every fader, trim, EQ and crossfader move in Open DJ is smoothed over about 10 ms, so fast hands do not produce clicks.
sources: W3C Web Audio API specification, AudioParam automation (setTargetAtTime, linearRampToValueAtTime)
Udo Zolzer (ed.), DAFX: Digital Audio Effects, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2011
entries.plain:
Audio is processed in blocks, called buffers. If a fader move is applied as a new number at the
start of each buffer, the gain jumps in steps. Each step is a tiny discontinuity in the wave,
heard as a click. Drag a fader and you get a rapid series of steps, one per buffer, which sounds
like a zipper or a buzz.

The cure is to never jump. When a gain changes, the engine slides from the old value to the new
one across many samples, per sample rather than per buffer. A linear ramp moves in a straight
line over a fixed time; a one-pole smoother eases in exponentially, covering about 63 percent of
the distance per time constant. A 10 ms ramp is short enough to feel instant and long enough to
be inaudible. "Ramp over one buffer" means the glide lasts exactly one block: at 1,024 frames
and 48 kHz that is about 21 ms.

entries.one_liner: How late each frequency comes out of a filter; when that lateness differs from band to band, the parts of a kick arrive apart and it smears.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Steep crossovers and EQs delay the bass more than the click, which softens kicks and can blur a mix of two tracks with different filters.
sources: Jens Blauert and Peter Laws, "Group delay distortions in electroacoustical systems", Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 63(5), 1978
Julius O. Smith III, "Introduction to Digital Filters with Audio Applications" (phase and group delay), CCRMA Stanford, https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/filters/
Wikipedia, "Group delay and phase delay" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
A filter changes not only how loud each frequency is but also when it comes out. Group delay is
that timing, measured per frequency, in milliseconds: how long the envelope of a sound at that
frequency is held back by the filter.

If the group delay is the same at every frequency, the whole sound is simply a bit late, which is
just latency and the shape survives. If it differs, the sound comes apart in time. A kick is a
low thump, a mid body and a high click that should land together; through a filter that delays
the lows more, the click arrives first and the thump trails behind, so the kick sounds softer and
smeared. Steep filters and high-Q filters have the largest delay near their cutoff.

The precise definition is the negative slope of the filter's phase response against frequency,
which is why "phase" and "delay" are discussed together. Our ears are least sensitive to it in
the bass, but differences of several milliseconds between bands can be heard on sharp drums.

entries.one_liner: A 70 BPM track and a 140 BPM track share every other beat, so they can be synced; the trick is choosing which octave to call it.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Sync can lock a deck at half or double the master's tempo, and analysis must pick the octave a DJ expects to see.
sources: Gouyon et al., An Experimental Comparison of Audio Tempo Induction Algorithms, IEEE Trans. Audio, Speech and Language Processing, 2006 (octave errors)
Pioneer DJ CDJ-3000 Operating Instructions (Beat Sync, half and double tempo), AlphaTheta
entries.plain:
Tempo has octaves, like pitch. A kick every beat at 70 BPM lines up exactly with every second
kick at 140 BPM, so the two can be mixed in time without changing either track much. The same
goes for a 174 BPM drum and bass track and an 87 BPM half-time groove: same pulse, different
counting. Beat trackers often land on the "wrong" octave, which is called an octave error.

To decide which octave to use, fold the tempo ratio by doubling or halving until it is as close
to 1 as it can get. The fair boundary is the square root of 2 (about 1.414): it sits exactly
halfway between 1 and 2 when you measure on a log scale, which is how both ears and pitch faders
work. A ratio above 1.414 is closer to 2 than to 1, so halve it; below 0.707, double it.

  example: 174 against 96 BPM, ratio 1.81 > 1.414

Sync does not use the square-root-of-2 cut. `_tempoRatioWithinRangeOrNull` in
`apps/webui/frontend/src/lib/rb/beat-sync-math.ts` tries the raw ratio, then half, then double,
and takes the first one inside the pitch range. In BAR mode a half or double lock is the
fallback, and it shows in orange because the bar count no longer holds. On the analysis side,
`apps/analysis_beatgrid/bpm.py` picks an octave inside a 70 to 180 BPM band, breaking ties toward
its geometric center of about 112 BPM, and `tempo_family.py` uses the genre tag so drum and
bass reads as 174, not 87.

entries.term: Hamiltonian path and the traveling salesman problem
entries.one_liner: Ordering a playlist is finding the cheapest route that visits every track once, with each hop costing how rough that transition is.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It explains why the current one-pass ordering leaves bad transitions at the end of a set, and what the planned optimizer does about it.
sources: Applegate, Bixby, Chvatal and Cook, The Traveling Salesman Problem, A Computational Study, Princeton University Press, 2006
Held and Karp, "A Dynamic Programming Approach to Sequencing Problems", Journal of SIAM 10(1), 1962
Wikipedia, "Travelling salesman problem" and "Hamiltonian path" (secondary pointers)
entries.plain:
Treat each track as a town and each transition as a road whose length is how rough that mix
would be. A set order is a route that visits every town exactly once, and the best order is the
shortest such route: a shortest Hamiltonian path. The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is the
famous version that returns home, a cycle. A DJ set is an open path instead, often with a fixed
opener and closer, and its roads are one-way: A into B is not the same mix as B into A. Trying
every order explodes (20 tracks have about 2.4 billion billion orders), so exact methods such as
Held-Karp only suit about a dozen tracks. Greedy picks the cheapest next track every time; it is
fast but strands the awkward tracks at the end. Two-ended growth works in from both the opener
and the closer, which spreads the leftovers. The cycle trick adds a dummy town that costs zero to
enter and leave, solves an ordinary loop, then cuts the loop at the dummy. Local moves such as
2-opt (reverse a stretch) and Or-opt (move one to three tracks) then polish the result.

                     spread out, no 9-cost cliff

entries.in_open_dj:
`apps/dj_copilot/solver.py` (PLAY IT) builds the order forward from one start with a beam of
width 8 and no improvement pass afterward. The playlist-ordering research (Tue 27 Oct 2026)
proposes an asymmetric open-path solver: contract locked pairs, add the zero-cost dummy, seed
from greedy runs plus the current beam result, polish with Or-opt and 2-opt, and use Held-Karp
on 12 or fewer tracks as the test oracle. Its first trap is "junk at the ends": fail when the
rate of abrupt edges in the last 20 percent is more than 1.5 times the rate in the middle.

entries.one_liner: Headroom is the space left below 0 dBFS; clipping is what happens when a signal runs out of it and the tops of the wave are cut flat.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Two decks playing together need more headroom than one, so Open DJ levels tracks below the ceiling and lights a clip warning just under full scale.
sources: IEC 60268-10, Peak programme level meters
EBU R128 (2023), permitted maximum true-peak level
Pioneer DJ DJM-900NXS2 operating instructions, channel level and master level indicators
entries.plain:
Headroom is the distance between where your music peaks and the ceiling, 0 dBFS. A track
peaking at -6 dBFS has 6 dB of headroom. Clipping is running out of it: the wave tries to go
higher than the system can represent, and its tops are sliced off flat. Flat tops add harsh
distortion, the crunchy, fizzy sound of a mixer "in the red".

DJ mixing eats headroom in a way single-track playback does not. When two tracks overlap, their
levels add, so a pair of tracks each peaking at -2 dBFS can sum well past 0. That is why
mixers ask you to keep channel meters out of the red, and why loud masters (which often peak
above 0 dBTP already) are trimmed down before they meet each other.

Clip warnings come from `apps/webui/frontend/src/lib/rb/meter-math.ts`, which latches the clip
light at -0.1 dBFS (`CLIP_DBFS`) rather than at exactly 0, since a sample of exactly full scale
is legal. The offline scan in `apps/loudness/scan.py` clamps any per-track gain to keep true
peak under a ceiling and flags when that clamp decided the number. The mixer itself computes in
floating point, so a sum above 1.0 is not cut until it is written to a fixed-point output, such
as the recorder and WAV writer in `apps/audio-engine/src/`, which clamp samples to -1 to 1.
I did not find a master limiter in the engine.

entries.one_liner: Tune a measure on one set of examples and judge it on another it never saw; grading on the tuning set flatters it.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Any pass mark Open DJ fits to ratings or labels is quoted from a held-out set, so the number predicts new tracks, not the ones it memorized.
sources: Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Springer, 2009 (chapter 7)
James, Witten, Hastie and Tibshirani, An Introduction to Statistical Learning, Springer, 2013 (chapter 5)
Wikipedia, "Training, validation, and test data sets" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
If you tune a measure on some examples and then grade it on the same ones, it looks great,
partly because it has learned their quirks rather than the general rule. That is overfitting.
So split the examples before you start. The fit set (training set) is where you choose weights
and thresholds, as often as you like. The held-out set (test set) is locked away during fitting
and scored once, at the end, and that score is the one you quote. Split by group, not by single
item: if one artist has tracks on both sides, the measure can learn that artist's sound and look
smarter than it is. And do not keep peeking. Tweaking until the held-out number looks good
quietly turns it into a second fit set; when that happens, collect a fresh one.

entries.one_liner: Loudness is read through three windows, the whole track (integrated), the last 3 s (short-term) and the last 400 ms (momentary).
entries.why_it_matters_here: A per-track trim uses integrated loudness, while judging a transition seam needs the short-term or momentary view of a few bars.
sources: ITU-R BS.1770-5 (2023), gating and integration of loudness
EBU Tech 3341, Loudness Metering, EBU Mode (defines M, S and I windows)
EBU Tech 3342, Loudness Range, a measure to supplement EBU R128 loudness normalisation
entries.plain:
The same LUFS measurement gives different answers depending on how long it listens.

- Momentary (M) averages the last 400 ms. It jumps with every kick and breakdown, like a fast
  meter.
- Short-term (S) averages the last 3 s, about one and a half bars at 128 BPM. It shows how loud
  a phrase feels.
- Integrated (I) covers the whole track. It is gated: blocks below -70 LUFS are ignored as
  silence, and then blocks more than 10 LU under the running average are ignored too, so a long
  quiet intro does not drag the figure down.

Loudness range (LRA, in LU) comes from the spread of short-term values, the 10th to 95th
percentile, so it says how much a track moves between quiet and loud passages. A flat club tool
might read 3 LU; a track with a long breakdown, 10 LU or more.

`apps/loudness/scan.py` keeps only the integrated figure and the loudness range from ffmpeg's

belong beside the waveform and in transition seam metrics.

entries.one_liner: One typed doorway every control walks through, so a button press and an agent command do exactly the same thing and both can be checked.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It is what makes Open DJ agent-native; a control that skips it works for your hand but is invisible to automation, tests and recordings.
sources: Gamma, Helm, Johnson, Vlissides, Design Patterns, Addison-Wesley, 1994 (the Command pattern)
Wikipedia, Inter-process communication, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-process_communication
entries.plain:
Every knob, fader and pad in the app sends a small typed message, such as "deck 2, set low EQ to
-12 dB", to one dispatcher. The dispatcher checks the message, queues it behind anything it must
wait for, runs it against the audio engine, and records the result. An agent or a test script
sends the very same message through the same door. Because there is one path, the state the
screen shows and the state an agent reads back can never disagree.

The precise term is a validated, serialized command dispatcher with a matching query surface.
"IPC" (inter-process communication) is loose here: most callers live in the same page.

entries.one_liner: A DJ EQ that splits the sound into bands with crossovers and gives each band its own volume, so a band can be turned down to silence.
entries.why_it_matters_here: A clean bass swap needs the outgoing bass gone, which an isolator does and Open DJ's current shelf EQ does not.
sources: Pioneer DJ, "DJM-900NXS2 Operating Instructions" (EQ curve selector, ISOLATOR and EQ settings), https://www.pioneerdj.com/
Allen and Heath, "Xone:92 User Guide" (EQ and total kill), https://www.allen-heath.com/
Siegfried Linkwitz, "Active Crossover Networks for Noncoincident Drivers", Journal of the Audio Engineering Society 24(1), 1976
entries.plain:
An isolator does not bend the sound with shelves and bells. It cuts the track into separate
bands with crossover filters, typically low, mid and high, sends each band through a plain volume
control, and adds the bands back together. With every knob at the center the bands sum back to
the original sound.

Because each band is its own path, turning a knob all the way down really removes that band: the
gain goes to zero, minus infinity in dB, and what remains is only the overlap at the crossover
slopes. That is the "kill" DJs use to drop the bass of one track while the other carries the
low end. The steeper the crossover, the cleaner the kill and the narrower the overlap, but steeper
crossovers delay some frequencies more than others, which is why their design matters.

Club rotary mixers and outboard isolator units made the sound famous; many modern club mixers
offer an isolator curve next to a classic EQ curve.

entries.one_liner: K-weighting is a two-stage filter that tilts audio toward what ears notice, lifting the highs and cutting deep bass, before loudness is measured.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It is why a bass-heavy techno track and a bright vocal track can share a LUFS figure while their peak meters disagree.
sources: ITU-R BS.1770-5 (2023), Annex 1, specification of the weighting filter
EBU Tech 3341, Loudness Metering, EBU Mode metering to supplement EBU R128
Wikipedia: LKFS, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LKFS (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
Ears are not equally sensitive across the spectrum. A lot of sub-bass energy moves the needle
on a plain energy meter but does not feel proportionally louder, while the presence range
around 2 to 5 kHz feels loud with little energy. If loudness were plain energy, bass-heavy
tracks would read too loud and get turned down too far.

K-weighting fixes that with two filters run before the energy is summed. Stage one is a high
shelf that adds about +4 dB above roughly 2 kHz, modeling the acoustic effect of a head.
Stage two is a gentle high-pass (the revised low-frequency B curve, RLB) that is about -6 dB
near 38 Hz and falls away below. Both are ordinary second-order biquad filters with
coefficients given in the standard for 48 kHz. Then each channel's power is averaged, summed and
turned into LUFS.

It is a deliberately simple model, cheaper than full psychoacoustic loudness, and it was
validated against listening tests on broadcast material.
entries.in_open_dj:
Open DJ does not implement the filter itself. The offline scan in `apps/loudness/scan.py` asks
ffmpeg's `ebur128` filter, which applies BS.1770 K-weighting inside its measurement, so every
LUFS figure in the library is K-weighted. The realtime channel meters in
`apps/webui/frontend/src/lib/rb/meter-math.ts` are peak and RMS meters with no K-weighting,
which is one reason a meter reading and a LUFS figure can disagree.

entries.one_liner: The sour rub when two playing tracks' notes disagree. Real, but usually third in line after the beat and the low end.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Key is the heaviest weight in Open DJ's track match score, but nothing yet listens to the actual overlap for dissonance.
sources: Mixed In Key, Harmonic Mixing book, https://mixedinkey.com/Book/
Plomp and Levelt, Tonal consonance and critical bandwidth, JASA, 1965
Wikipedia, Consonance and dissonance (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
A key clash is what you hear when two tracks play notes that do not belong together: a sour,
wobbly rub, worst on long held chords and basslines. Physically, two close but unequal pitches
beat against each other inside the ear's hearing bands, and that roughness reads as tension.
The worst pairs are a semitone or a tritone apart, which on the Camelot wheel are five and six
steps away.

When is it third-order, a smaller problem than it sounds? Most transitions fail first on the
beat (drums out of phase) and second on the low end (two kicks or basslines stacked, too loud).
Key matters after those, and it can almost vanish when the overlap is a few bars, when one track
is mostly drums, when the DJ has EQ'd the melodic parts of one track out, or when the detector's
key was a low-confidence guess anyway. It matters most for long, melodic blends and for two
vocals.

entries.one_liner: How sure a key detector is about its answer. A low-confidence key is a guess and should not filter or rank your tracks.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ flags a low-confidence key as no_tonal_center and leaves it inert instead of letting a guess pass as a finding.
sources: Krumhansl, Cognitive Foundations of Musical Pitch, Oxford University Press, 1990
Mueller, Fundamentals of Music Processing, Springer, 2nd ed. 2021, tonal analysis chapter
Mixed In Key, Harmonic Mixing book, https://mixedinkey.com/Book/
entries.plain:
A key detector never says "I don't know" on its own. It compares the track's notes against all
24 keys and always returns the best match, even for a drum loop with no tune. Confidence is how
well that winner actually matched. A second number matters just as much: the margin, how far the
winner beat the runner-up. If the top two are nearly tied, the detector flipped a coin.

Low confidence happens on drones, noise intros, percussion-only tools, tracks that change key,
and modal music that does not fit major or minor templates. The runner-up is usually the relative
key or a fifth away, which is why detectors disagree with each other in those directions.

A low-confidence key should not drive a decision because a wrong key fails twice: it hides good
tracks from the suggester and recommends ones that clash. Showing the key with a warning is
honest; ranking by it is not.

`apps/analysis_key/flags.py` raises `no_tonal_center` when either the winning correlation or the

entries.one_liner: With key lock on, the pitch fader changes the tempo and leaves the key alone; with it off, faster also means higher.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Key lock decides whether a deck goes through the time stretcher, which changes its latency, CPU cost and sound.
sources: Pioneer DJ CDJ-3000 Operating Instructions (Master Tempo), AlphaTheta
rekordbox Operating Instructions (Master Tempo), AlphaTheta / Pioneer DJ
Serato DJ Pro Software Manual (Keylock), Serato
entries.plain:
On a turntable, pushing the pitch fader up makes the record play faster and sound higher, like
a tape sped up. Key lock (Pioneer calls it Master Tempo) keeps the musical key where it was while
the tempo moves. That lets you push a track 5 percent faster to match another deck and still mix
it harmonically, and stops vocals turning into chipmunks.

Under the hood, key lock off is plain varispeed: resampling, cheap and with no delay. Key lock
on hands the deck to a time stretcher, which costs CPU and a few tens of milliseconds of latency
and can soften drums slightly. Many DJs leave it off for small changes and turn it on for big
ones. The pitch shift with key lock off is 12 x log2(tempo ratio) semitones.

entries.one_liner: A lane is one control drawn as a curve across the mix; a preset is a saved setting for every lane at once.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Lanes make a transition editable and visible; presets and Open DJ's styles make it one tap, and are the menu an automatic mixer chooses from.
sources: Spotify Support, Mixed playlists, https://support.spotify.com/us/article/mixed-playlists/
Spotify Newsroom, Mix your favorite playlists, Tue 19 Aug 2025, https://newsroom.spotify.com/2025-08-19/mix-your-favorite-playlists-seamlessly-by-adding-your-own-transitions/
entries.plain:
Spotify's Mix editor shows a transition as five lanes under the two waveforms: Volume, EQ,
Filter, Effects and Looping. Each lane is a curve, or a choice of curve, for one thing that moves
during the blend, the way automation lanes work in a music DAW. A preset fills in all the lanes at
once. The picker, as seen live on Tue 27 Oct 2026, offers Fade, Rise, Blend, Wave, Melt, Slam,
Dissolve, Surge, Afterglow and No transition, plus Auto and Custom; Spotify's own pages name only
the first three. Picking a preset fills every lane (none of the nine captured presets uses the
Effects or Looping lane), while Custom lets you pick per lane.

A DJ does all five by hand at once: faders, EQ knobs, a filter, an effect, a loop. Lanes simply
write that down.

entries.one_liner: A crossover filter pair whose low and high outputs add back to a perfectly flat level, because each is 6 dB down at the crossover and in phase.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It is the standard way to build an isolator EQ whose bands add back to the original track with no bump at the crossover.
sources: Siegfried Linkwitz, "Active Crossover Networks for Noncoincident Drivers", Journal of the Audio Engineering Society 24(1), 1976
Rane Corporation, "Linkwitz-Riley Crossovers: A Primer" (RaneNote 160), https://www.ranecommercial.com/
Linkwitz Lab, "Crossovers", https://www.linkwitzlab.com/
entries.plain:
When you split a track into bands and add them back, you want the original. A plain Butterworth
low-pass and high-pass at the same frequency are each 3 dB down at the crossover; since they come
out in phase there (for the usual 4th-order case), their amplitudes add, 0.707 + 0.707 = 1.41, and
you get a 3 dB bump right at the crossover.

Siegfried Linkwitz and Russ Riley fixed this in 1976 by squaring a Butterworth filter: put two
identical Butterworth filters in a row. Each band is now 6 dB down at the crossover (amplitude
0.5), the two outputs stay in phase with each other at every frequency, and 0.5 + 0.5 = 1. The sum
is flat. The common version, LR4, is two cascaded 2nd-order Butterworth sections per side and
falls at 24 dB per octave.

Flat in level does not mean untouched: the summed signal is an all-pass, so its phase still turns
around the crossover and the lows arrive slightly later than the highs.
entries.picture:
what you hear around the crossover fc when the bands are summed

 Butterworth pair, each -3 dB at fc:
  +3 dB |                  .***.          <- sum bumps up 3 dB
   0 dB |*****************       *****************
        |          low -3 dB  x  -3 dB high

 Linkwitz-Riley pair, each -6 dB at fc:
   0 dB |*****************************************  <- sum is flat
  -6 dB |          low -6 dB  x  -6 dB high
        +--------------------+-------------------> Hz
                             fc

 LR4 = Butterworth 2nd order > Butterworth 2nd order (same fc)
entries.in_open_dj:
The colored waveform builds each band edge from two cascaded 2-pole Butterworth biquads at the
same frequency (`apps/audio-engine/src/waveform.rs`), which is the textbook LR4 recipe, though the
waveform only measures band energy and never sums the bands back. The live deck EQ has no
crossover yet; an isolator mode would be the place an LR crossover lands.

entries.one_liner: A beat loop that only lasts while you hold the pad, with slip on, so the track picks up on time the moment you let go.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Rolls are the classic build into a drop; done right they need beat loops, halving and slip working together on the grid.
sources: Serato DJ Pro Software Manual (Roll pad mode), Serato
Pioneer DJ CDJ-3000 Operating Instructions (Beat Loop, Slip Loop), AlphaTheta
entries.plain:
Hold a roll pad and the deck repeats a short slice, 1 beat or 1/2 or 1/8, starting on the grid.
Let go and the track carries on as if nothing happened, because slip kept the song running
underneath. The classic use is a build: roll 1 beat, then 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, each halving faster
and more urgent, then release right on the drop, or stop a beat early and let one beat of silence
set the drop up. Because of slip, the drop arrives exactly where it was always going to.

Precisely: a roll is a momentary, quantized beat loop with slip engaged, and loop halving shrinks
the loop around its start while the hidden playhead keeps advancing.

entries.one_liner: The instant a loop jumps from its end back to its start; if the waveform does not match there, you hear a click.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Beat loops and rolls cross the seam every repeat, so a click there repeats on every beat the DJ holds the loop.
sources: Zolzer (ed.), DAFX: Digital Audio Effects, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2011 (crossfades and discontinuities)
Roads, The Computer Music Tutorial, MIT Press, 1996 (looping and splice points in samplers)
entries.plain:
A loop plays a stretch of audio, then jumps back to the start and plays it again. That jump is
the seam. Sound is a wave, and if the wave is high at the loop's end and low at its start, the
speaker is asked to move from one to the other in a single sample. That sudden step is a click,
and in a short loop it clicks on every repeat, which turns a clean roll into a ticking mess.

Two classic fixes. Put the loop points where the wave crosses zero, so both sides of the jump are
near silence (it helps, but a beat-accurate loop rarely lands on a zero crossing in both
channels). Or crossfade: for a few milliseconds around the seam, fade the loop's tail out while
fading its head in, so the jump is spread over hundreds of samples instead of one.
entries.picture:
the seam, sample by sample (stereo left channel)

  loop end ...  0.55  0.68  0.80  |  -0.30 -0.21 -0.10  ... loop start
                                  ^ seam: a step of 1.10 in one sample
                                    = a broadband click, every repeat

fix 1, zero crossings: move both points to where the wave is near 0
          ...  0.04  0.01  0.00  |   0.00  0.02  0.05  ...  no step

fix 2, crossfade the seam over a few ms:
  tail of loop    ######======------.....         fading out
  head of loop    .....------======######         fading in
                  |<-------- 5 ms ------->|       no step to hear

entries.one_liner: Loudness continuity scores a transition by the largest LU gap between the mix's loudness and a straight line from the outgoing to the incoming track.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It turns "the blend surged" or "the room dropped" into one number an automatic transition can be tuned against.
sources: ITU-R BS.1770-5 (2023), loudness measurement
EBU Tech 3341, Loudness Metering (short-term 3 s window)
Open DJ proposal for a rendered-transition scorer (project source, not yet on main, not a public standard)
entries.plain:
A good transition hands the room from one track to the next without the level jumping. If the
outgoing track sits at -9 LUFS and the incoming one at -11 LUFS, the ideal seam drifts smoothly
from -9 to -11 across the overlap: a straight line. Loudness continuity measures how far the
real mix strays from that line.

The method: render the transition, measure loudness through it in short windows (short-term,
3 s, or per bar), draw the straight line between the two tracks' own levels, and report the
largest gap in LU, above or below. A bump from both faders being open shows up as a positive
gap; a hole from pulling one fader too early shows up as a negative gap. Smaller is better, and
0 LU is a perfect hand-over.

continuity = max over t of | L_mix(t) - line(t) |

aliases: loudness units relative to full scale
entries.one_liner: LUFS is a loudness level on a scale built to match hearing; LU is a step on it, and one LU equals one dB.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ scans every track to an integrated LUFS figure, and seam metrics for transitions are expressed in LU rather than raw dB.
sources: ITU-R BS.1770-5 (2023), Algorithms to measure audio programme loudness and true-peak audio level
EBU R128 (2023), Loudness normalisation and permitted maximum level of audio signals
EBU Tech 3341, Loudness Metering, EBU Mode metering to supplement EBU R128
entries.plain:
Peak meters say how high a wave goes; they do not say how loud it feels. A quiet track with one
sharp snare can peak higher than a dense, compressed track that feels twice as loud. LUFS
(Loudness Units relative to Full Scale) measures what people hear: it weights the audio the way
ears do (K-weighting), averages the energy, and skips silence. ITU-R BS.1770 defines it, and the
US name LKFS is the same thing.

A level is written in LUFS, and a difference between two levels is written in LU. One LU is one
dB, so a track at -8 LUFS needs -6 dB of trim to sit with one at -14 LUFS. Common targets are
-23 LUFS for broadcast (EBU R128) and about -14 LUFS for streaming services; club masters
often measure -9 to -6 LUFS integrated.

loudness = -0.691 + 10 * log10(sum of K-weighted channel power)

`apps/loudness/scan.py` measures one file with ffmpeg's `ebur128` filter (run as a separate

`apps/analysis_loudness/` wraps that scan as an analysis lane and backfills it across the
