entries.one_liner: Minimum-phase filters react instantly but bend timing per frequency; linear-phase filters keep timing even but add latency and pre-ringing.
entries.why_it_matters_here: A live DJ EQ must be minimum phase for low latency, so its timing smear is a design fact to manage, not a bug to fix.
sources: Julius O. Smith III, "Introduction to Digital Filters with Audio Applications" (minimum phase, linear phase), CCRMA Stanford, https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/filters/
Richard G. Lyons, "Understanding Digital Signal Processing", 3rd edition, Prentice Hall, 2010
Bob Katz, "Mastering Audio: The Art and the Science", Focal Press, 2015 (linear-phase equalizers)
entries.plain:
Feed a filter a single click and watch what comes out: that is its impulse response, and its
shape tells you the filter's phase family.

A minimum-phase filter puts its energy out as early as possible. The click is answered at once,
then the tail dies away. There is no added latency, which is why every analog EQ and every biquad
in a DJ mixer works this way. The cost is that the delay differs by frequency, so phase bends
around each cutoff and transients are slightly smeared.

A linear-phase filter answers with a symmetric shape centered some time later. Every frequency is
delayed by exactly the same amount, so a drum hit keeps its shape. But the filter has to wait half
its own length before answering, often tens of milliseconds for bass, and the symmetric response
puts a little ringing before each hit as well as after it, which is audible as pre-echo on steep
low cuts. Mastering engineers use it; live mixing cannot afford the wait.

entries.in_open_dj:
Every live filter is minimum phase: the shelves, bell, low-pass and high-pass are IIR biquads in
`apps/audio-engine/src/dsp.rs`. No linear-phase FIR filter exists in the live path. The only
phase-neutral filtering is the offline zero-phase pass in `scripts/bench/r1-offline/`.

entries.one_liner: The mix region is the stretch of bars where two tracks overlap; the mix point is the downbeat inside it where the handover happens.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Picking the region and point is most of what makes an automatic transition sound chosen rather than random.
sources: Spotify Support, Mixed playlists, https://support.spotify.com/us/article/mixed-playlists/
Spotify Newsroom, Mix your favorite playlists, Tue 19 Aug 2025, https://newsroom.spotify.com/2025-08-19/mix-your-favorite-playlists-seamlessly-by-adding-your-own-transitions/
entries.plain:
When two tracks blend there is a window where both are playing. Spotify's Mix editor calls this
stretch the mix region and offers lengths of 2, 4 or 8 bars when it has found a beat grid. Inside
it sits the mix point, a downbeat where the incoming track takes over. In the editor you drag the
waveform to move the point, and the region moves with it. The editor's green vertical line is the
preview playhead, not the point: the point is the region's center, where every preset's steps land
and the stop button sits. Spotify does not document the shape, but
the editor's curves show the region centered on the point: the incoming track rises across the first half, the outgoing falls across
the second.

DJs say the same thing as: where you mix in, how long you blend, and the bar the new track
takes over.
entries.in_open_dj:
Not yet as a feature. AutoPlay on main does a hard cut with a low-EQ duck, not a chosen region.
The AutoDJ research (`(private path)`) plans
`get_mix_windows(track_id, role)`: ranked mix-out windows on outros or breakdowns and mix-in

entries.one_liner: Robert Moog's resonant 24 dB per octave low-pass, four stages with feedback, the warm squelchy sound many DJ filter sweeps imitate.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It is the reference for the character a resonant DJ filter sweep is expected to have, which Open DJ's plain filter knob does not yet aim for.
sources: Robert A. Moog, US Patent 3,475,623, "Electronic high-pass and low-pass filters employing the base to emitter diode resistance of bipolar transistors", 1969
Tim Stilson and Julius O. Smith, "Analyzing the Moog VCF with Considerations for Digital Implementation", International Computer Music Conference, 1996
Antti Huovilainen, "Non-linear Digital Implementation of the Moog Ladder Filter", DAFx, 2004
entries.plain:
In the 1960s Robert Moog built a low-pass filter from a ladder of transistor pairs: four simple
6 dB per octave stages in a row, giving 24 dB per octave. The trick is a feedback path that takes
the output, flips it, and adds it back at the input. Turn that feedback up and the filter
resonates: a peak grows at the cutoff, the sound gets vocal and squelchy, and near the top of the
range it starts to sing a pure tone of its own, called self-oscillation.

Two quirks are part of its sound. As resonance rises the bass below the cutoff gets quieter,
because the feedback works against the passband. And the transistors saturate on loud input, a
soft distortion that makes sweeps sound warm rather than clinical. Digital models try to keep both;
a plain biquad has neither.

DJ mixers and software filters with a resonance knob often borrow this behavior, so "Moog-style"
has become shorthand for a resonant, slightly driven low-pass sweep.

entries.one_liner: Break the thing on purpose and check the test goes red; a check you have never seen fail has not been shown to work.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Every quality measure we score transitions with must drop when we inject a known defect, or it is not measuring that defect.
sources: DeMillo, Lipton and Sayward, "Hints on Test Data Selection", IEEE Computer 11(4), 1978
Jia and Harman, "An Analysis and Survey of the Development of Mutation Testing", IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 37(5), 2011
Wikipedia, "Mutation testing" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
A test that passes proves little until you have watched it fail. Mutation testing makes the
failure happen on purpose: change the code or the input in one small, known way (a "mutant"),
run the check, and expect it to go red. If it stays green, the mutant "survived", and that is a
finding: the check carries an assumption nothing verifies. The same idea applies to a quality
measure. Take a good transition and inject a defect a DJ would hear (shift deck B by 30 ms,
bring it in one beat late, clash two vocals, add a click at a loop seam), then score it again.
The score must drop by more than its noise band, or the measure is blind to that defect. Mutate
the opposite way too: a fix that overshoots (punishing every vocal overlap, say) also needs a
control that shows the original good behavior still scores well.

fixture's noise band before the measure is used to judge anything.

entries.one_liner: The noise band is how far a number wobbles when nothing changed; the bootstrap measures that wobble by resampling your own results.
entries.why_it_matters_here: A round that claims to improve a transition score or a latency only counts if the change is bigger than the noise band.
sources: Efron and Tibshirani, An Introduction to the Bootstrap, Chapman and Hall, 1993
Efron, "Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife", Annals of Statistics 7(1), 1979
Wikipedia, "Bootstrapping (statistics)" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
Measure the same thing twice and you get two slightly different numbers: a different sample of
tracks, timer jitter, a busy machine. The noise band is how far the number wanders when nothing
real has changed, and a change smaller than that is not evidence of anything. You can find it by
repeating the run, but repeats are slow. The bootstrap gets an estimate from the results you
already have: with n results, draw n of them at random with replacement (so some repeat and some
drop out), recompute the metric, and do that a couple of thousand times. The middle 95 percent of
those recomputed values is a 95 percent confidence interval. It needs no formula for how the
metric is distributed, which is why it suits odd metrics like a p95 or an AUC. The working rule:
call a result better only when the new interval clears the old value, or the change exceeds the
noise band measured on the same fixtures.

   ... 2000 times, keep the middle 95 percent as the interval
entries.in_open_dj:
The macro quality measure research (Tue 27 Oct 2026) makes the noise band part of every round:
each round reports its before and after on the same scorer version and fixtures with the delta
and its noise band; a round that moves M by less than the noise band twice in a row must change
hypothesis class; and AUC targets come with bootstrapped confidence intervals. The round log in
`apps/analysis_bench/rounds.py` refuses a round without controls. I did not find a shared
bootstrap helper in the code yet; it would belong beside that round log.

entries.one_liner: Playing a transition into a file as fast as the computer can, instead of out of the speakers in real time, so it can be measured.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It lets Open DJ score many candidate transitions in seconds and get the same answer every time, before anything reaches the crowd.
sources: W3C, Web Audio API, OfflineAudioContext, https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/
Udo Zoelzer (ed.), DAFX Digital Audio Effects, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2011
entries.plain:
Live playback has to keep up with the clock on the wall: one second of music takes one second.
An offline render runs the same mixing math on a pretend clock that moves as fast as the CPU
allows, writing the result to a file instead of the speakers. A 30 second transition might take
a fraction of a second. Because nothing waits for the sound card, the same plan renders to the
same bytes every time, which is what you want when you are comparing options or catching a
regression.

The trade is that an offline render is a preview, not the performance. The live engine still
has to play it on the real clock, so the two should be compared, not assumed equal.

entries.in_open_dj:
The Rust engine renders plans offline: `odj-audio render --plan PLAN.json --out OUT.wav`, with
`--decks-out DIR` for each deck's own audio (`apps/audio-engine/src/offline.rs`,
`src/bin/odj-audio.rs`). Blocks split at every event and ramp step, so timing never depends on
block size. Besides the mix it reports which decks are heard over time, where they overlap, how
long each plays alone either side, and each deck's tempo. Today it refuses stems and beat sync,
so stem-aware transitions cannot be previewed yet.

entries.one_liner: Finding the exact moments notes and drum hits start. Sharp onsets are the ruler for checking a beat grid or an alignment.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ stores onset times per track and uses them to propose hot cues and to spot a beat grid that starts in the wrong place.
sources: Bello et al., A Tutorial on Onset Detection in Music Signals, IEEE Transactions on Speech and Audio Processing, 2005
Mueller, Fundamentals of Music Processing, Springer, 2nd ed. 2021, onset detection
Wikipedia, Onset (audio) (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
An onset is the instant something starts: a kick lands, a hat ticks, a piano key goes down.
Detecting onsets means scanning the audio for sudden rises in energy. The common recipe is
spectral flux: cut the audio into short frames, compare each frame's spectrum to the one before,
add up only the increases, and pick the peaks of that curve. Drums give tall, narrow peaks; a
slow pad fading in gives almost none.

Onsets anchor alignment measurements because they are the sharpest events in a track. If you
want to know whether a beat grid sits on the kick or 12 milliseconds late, or whether two decks
are truly in phase, you compare grid lines to onset times. A sustained chord has no single
moment to measure against; a kick does. Onsets are also where a cue point feels right to a DJ,
because pressing play on one starts the track with a hit, not mid-note.

entries.in_open_dj:
Analysis records carry `onsets_s`. `apps/analysis/detect_bad_beatgrid.py` compares the first
transient to the first downbeat to flag a grid that starts in the wrong place, and
`apps/analysis/auto_cues.py` proposes hot cues by picking the loudest onset in each time bin and
snapping it to a nearby downbeat.

entries.one_liner: p95 is the time that 95 of every 100 tries beat; it shows the slow tail that an average hides.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ writes its latency targets as p95 numbers, so a rare slow deck load or a late beat counts against us instead of vanishing into an average.
sources: Dean and Barroso, "The Tail at Scale", Communications of the ACM 56(2), 2013
Hyndman and Fan, "Sample Quantiles in Statistical Packages", The American Statistician 50(4), 1996
Wikipedia, "Percentile" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
Sort every measurement from fastest to slowest. The p50, or median, is the one halfway down the
list; the p95 is the one 95 percent of the way down. The mean (the plain average) lets many fast
tries cancel a few awful ones: 99 deck loads of 100 ms and one of 3 s average out to 129 ms,
which looks fine, yet the DJ felt the 3 s one, mid-set. Latency is a tail problem, because the
one late beat is the one the floor hears, so we promise on p95 (sometimes p99) and quote the p50
beside it for the typical case. A percentile also needs enough samples to mean anything: a p95
taken from 10 runs is really "the second slowest run", so always state how many runs it came
from.
entries.in_open_dj:
`(private path)` states its user-facing targets as percentiles: the library
filter keystroke-to-render target is p95 at or under 50 ms (S7), and waveform smoothness is a
p95 frame delta at or under the display refresh interval (S4). KPI names such as
`latency.input_to_audible_p95_ms` and `latency.deck_load_playable_p95_ms` carry the percentile
in the name, and the same spec's denominator-honesty rule applies to every quoted p95. The
transitions research uses p95 twice: the scorer reads beat offset between the two decks at p95,
so a single flammed kick cannot hide among good ones, and the try-er must return candidates in
p50 2.0 s and p95 3.0 s over 20 runs. New work on a latency path gets a row in
`(private path)` until it is measured.

entries.one_liner: Record what the live engine actually played and compare it with the offline render of the same plan, within a stated tolerance.
entries.why_it_matters_here: The scorer judges the offline render, so the score only describes what the crowd hears if live playback matches that render.
sources: Feathers, Working Effectively with Legacy Code, Prentice Hall, 2004 (characterization tests)
EBU Tech 3341, Loudness Metering, EBU, 2016 (loudness units used for the level tolerance)
Wikipedia, "Regression testing" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
To judge a transition quickly we render it offline: the computer works out the mixed audio
faster than real time, with no speakers involved, and the scorer measures that file. But the DJ
hears the live engine, which has its own clock, buffers and scheduling. If the two disagree, the
score is about a sound nobody heard. A parity capture closes that gap: play the same plan on the
same tracks through the live path, record what actually came out, line it up with the render,
and compare what matters, mainly when each beat lands and how loud it is. Pass means every
difference stays inside a stated tolerance; fail means the live path drifts, and that is a bug
in playback, not in the transition. Note the name clash: `apps/parity` is something else, it
scores our track analysis against rekordbox's.

entries.one_liner: How sync keeps two decks in step over time: ignore tiny errors, nudge the tempo for small ones, and seek when they are far apart.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Matching BPM once is not enough; grids and clocks drift, and this loop is what stops a synced mix from slowly flamming.
sources: Astrom and Murray, Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers, Princeton University Press, 2008 (proportional control, deadband, saturation)
Pioneer DJ CDJ-3000 Operating Instructions (Beat Sync), AlphaTheta
entries.plain:
Two decks set to the same BPM still wander apart: the grids are not perfect, tempos inside a
track drift, and measurements jitter. Phase correction is the small loop that keeps checking
"how far apart are the beats right now?" and steers. It works like a driver keeping a lane:
ignore a tiny wobble, steer gently for a small drift, and if you are way off, stop and re-place
the car instead of swerving.

The precise parts are a dead band (errors this small get no correction, so the loop does not
chase its own noise), a proportional nudge (a tempo trim sized to the error), a cap on that trim
(so it never becomes an audible pitch bend), and a seek (a jump) when the error is too big to
walk back in time. The trim is roughly: trim = error / correction window, then clamped to the
cap.

  -15        -2    0    +2                  +15
---+----------+----+----+-------------------+--------->
 SEEK | nudge  | dead band | nudge, capped   | SEEK
      |        |  no trim  |                 |

inside +-2 ms     play the base sync tempo exactly
2 to 15 ms        trim the tempo to remove the error over 4 beats,
                  never more than 0.3 % of the base tempo
past 15 ms or     lock lost: re-join with one seek, which is quicker
a quarter beat    than walking the error back for half a minute
entries.in_open_dj:
This is `apps/webui/frontend/src/lib/rb/phase-lock.ts`. The dead band is 2 ms
(`PHASE_LOCK_DEADBAND_MS`); once trimming, it holds until the error is under 1 ms, so an error
sitting on the edge does not flip on and off. The nudge corrects over 4 master beats, the trim
cap is 0.3 percent (`PHASE_LOCK_MAX_TRIM` in `beat-sync-math.ts`, about 5 cents), and a re-join
seek happens past 15 ms or a quarter beat, confirmed over 3 ticks and no sooner than 8 seconds
after the last join. Uneven rekordbox dynamic grids are read through a smoothed copy so the lock
does not chase their 5 to 10 ms steps.

entries.one_liner: Whether an effect or a tap sits before or after the channel fader decides whether pulling the fader also kills the effect's tail.
entries.why_it_matters_here: An echo out only works if the echo keeps ringing after the fader closes, so where the effect sits is a design choice, not a detail.
sources: AlphaTheta, DJM-900NXS2 Operating Instructions (Beat FX and channel routing), https://www.pioneerdj.com/
Wikipedia, Aux-send, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aux-send
entries.plain:
On a mixer channel the signal flows through trim, EQ and then the channel fader. An effect can
be patched in before the fader or after it. Before the fader, closing the fader silences
everything the effect produced too, so an echo dies the instant you pull down. After the fader,
the fader feeds the effect, and an echo already in its delay line keeps repeating and fading
naturally. That is the classic echo out: hit echo, pull the fader, let the repeats carry the
room into the next track.

Headphone cue is the opposite case: it listens before the fader on purpose, so you can hear a
track that the room cannot.

  fader pulled at bar 8
  dry    ########|
  echo   ########|              tail cut dead
                 ^ fader closes

  POST-FADER effect, tail keeps its own output
  deck > TRIM > EQ > FADER > ECHO > master
  fader pulled at bar 8
  dry    ########|
  echo   ########|# # # . . .   repeats decay on their own

Not yet for effects: the beat FX rack (delay, echo, reverb) is planned, not built
(`apps/webui/frontend/src/lib/rb/planned-explainers.ts`). The taps already follow the rule:

and the headphone cue tap is post-EQ and pre-fader (`lib/rb/audio-engine-types.ts`). When echo
lands, it has to sit after the fader or on a send for echo out to work.

entries.one_liner: Q sets how narrow and peaked a filter is; push it high and the filter rings at its cutoff, the squelchy whistle of a resonant sweep.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ's filter knob uses a fixed low Q with no resonance control yet, and its mid bell uses Q = 1.
sources: Robert Bristow-Johnson, "Audio EQ Cookbook" (Q, bandwidth and slope), W3C note, https://www.w3.org/TR/audio-eq-cookbook/
W3C, "Web Audio API", BiquadFilterNode Q attribute, https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/
Wikipedia, "Q factor" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
Q, the quality factor, measures how sharply a filter is tuned. On a bell EQ it is the center
frequency divided by the width of the bell: Q = 1 is broad and musical, Q = 10 is a narrow
surgical notch or spike.

On a low-pass or high-pass, Q shapes the corner. At about 0.7 the corner is smooth with no bump
(the Butterworth shape). Raise it and a peak grows right at the cutoff: that band is boosted
above everything else. This is the resonance knob on a synth or a DJ filter, and sweeping a
resonant peak through a track gives the classic squelchy, vocal "wow".

High Q rings. A sharply tuned filter keeps sounding at its own frequency after the input moves on,
like a struck bell, because it stores energy and lets it out slowly. The ring dies away over
roughly Q divided by (pi times the frequency) seconds: at Q = 10 and 200 Hz, about 16 ms, long
enough to blur a kick. Push resonance far enough and some filters ring forever, which is
self-oscillation.

entries.one_liner: Quantize moves a cue, loop or jump you trigger a little early or late onto the nearest beat on the grid, so it still lands in time.
entries.why_it_matters_here: With quantize on, a hot cue or beat jump pressed slightly off still lands on the beat, as long as the grid itself is right.
sources: rekordbox Operating Instructions (Quantize), AlphaTheta / Pioneer DJ
Serato DJ Pro Software Manual (Quantize), Serato
entries.plain:
Human hands are a few tens of milliseconds sloppy, and ears notice. Quantize lets the software
fix that: when you press a hot cue, set a loop or jump, it moves the action onto the beat grid.
There are two flavors. For a point you are setting (a loop in point, a cue), it snaps to the
nearest grid line. For an action that starts playback or jumps while playing, it waits for the
next beat (or bar) and fires exactly there.

The catch is that quantize can only be as good as the grid. On a badly gridded track it
confidently snaps everything to the wrong place, which is worse than no quantize at all.

entries.plain:
Rachel M. Bittner is a music-information-retrieval researcher at Spotify in New York, a research
manager for applied machine learning on audio by 2022 after joining as a research scientist. Her
PhD is from NYU's Music and Audio Research Laboratory (MARL), with Juan Pablo Bello.

Worth remembering:

- MedleyDB (ISMIR 2014): a multitrack dataset with pitch and melody annotations, built so melody
  extraction research had real mixes to learn from. Still a standard benchmark.
- Automatic Playlist Sequencing and Transitions (ISMIR 2017, with Gu, Hernandez, Humphrey, Jehan,
  McCurry and Montecchio, all Spotify): sequence a playlist as a path through pairwise
  compatibility, then plan each transition; beat-tracking errors were the number one failure,
  and an A/B test with hand-made transitions lifted daily return by 1.4 percentage points. This
  brief treats it as the floor on method, not a description of what Spotify ships today.
- mirdata (2019 onward, co-author): the Python library of dataset loaders that made MIR datasets
  reproducible to load, including MedleyDB.
- Basic Pitch (2022): Spotify's open-source, instrument-agnostic, polyphonic audio-to-MIDI
  converter with pitch bends, from an ICASSP 2022 paper; runs faster than real time on a laptop.

Links: the paper PDF, the Spotify newsroom interview, the Basic Pitch repository and the anthology
page of her ISMIR papers are in the sources list. A LinkedIn profile was not verified here.

entries.one_liner: Relative keys share all seven notes (8A and 8B). Parallel keys share a root but not a mood (A minor and A major).
entries.why_it_matters_here: The relative swap is a default-on match in Open DJ's key filter, while a parallel swap is a bigger move it does not offer by default.
sources: Mixed In Key, Harmonic Mixing book, https://mixedinkey.com/Book/
Mixed In Key, Camelot Wheel, https://mixedinkey.com/camelot-wheel/
Wikipedia, Relative key and Parallel key (secondary pointers)
entries.plain:
Every major key has a minor twin built from exactly the same seven notes. C major and A minor
use only the white keys of a piano; the difference is which note feels like home. On the Camelot
wheel the twins sit on the same number: 8B and 8A. Swapping between them is called a relative
move, and it is the smoothest mood change in DJing: the notes stay, the color shifts from bright
to moody or back.

A parallel pair is different: same home note, different scale. A minor (8A) and A major (11B)
both resolve to A, but three notes move up a semitone (C, F and G become C#, F# and G#). On the
wheel that is three steps away plus a letter change, so it is not "adjacent". Some DJs use the
parallel swap on purpose for a sudden lift, usually over a short overlap or a vocal hook, because
holding two tracks in parallel keys for 32 bars lets those three notes rub.

The `relative` rule in `CAMELOT_RULES` (`apps/shared/harmonic.py`) matches 8A to 8B and back and

tags, `apps/analysis_bench/scorers/key_lane.py` treats a relative, parallel or fifth-apart answer
as a related miss rather than a flat wrong one, because detectors confuse these pairs most often.

entries.one_liner: ReplayGain is a loudness tag stored in a file that tells a player how much to turn that track up or down so tracks play at an even level.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ measures loudness the same way but applies the result as a mixer trim the DJ can see and override, not as a hidden playback tag.
sources: ReplayGain 2.0 specification, wiki.hydrogenaud.io (ReplayGain 2.0 specification page)
Mixxx User Manual 2.5, glossary and Normalization preferences, manual.mixxx.org
entries.plain:
ReplayGain is a player-side normalization scheme from the early 2000s. A scanner measures each
track once and writes two numbers into its tags: a gain in dB (track gain, or album gain for a
whole album played together) and the track's peak. The player reads the tag at playback and
scales the audio, without changing the file. Version 2.0 uses the BS.1770 loudness measurement
with a reference of -18 LUFS, so a track at -12 LUFS gets a tag of about -6 dB.

LUFS trim does the same arithmetic. The differences are where it lives and who sees it.
ReplayGain is silent and global: every track arrives levelled, and the tag can be wrong or
missing. A DJ trim is a visible knob per deck, set from the measured LUFS against a chosen
target, which the DJ can ride during the mix. ReplayGain also has no say in a blend; it levels
tracks in isolation, not two tracks playing at once.

Open DJ does not read or write ReplayGain tags. `apps/loudness/scan.py` derives a

result cannot push true peak past the ceiling. The intended consumer is the per-deck trim, as
rekordbox and Serato do with auto-gain. Mixxx, by contrast, applies ReplayGain-based
normalization by default, per its manual.

entries.one_liner: A chooser sees a state, takes an action, gets a reward from the environment, and its policy is the rule it improves.
entries.why_it_matters_here: The transition chooser is framed as a policy iterating against one score, so the score has to be trustworthy before the chooser is tuned against it.
sources: Sutton and Barto, Reinforcement Learning, An Introduction, 2nd ed., MIT Press, 2018 (chapter 3)
Amodei et al., "Concrete Problems in AI Safety", arXiv 1606.06565, 2016 (reward hacking)
Wikipedia, "Reinforcement learning" (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
Reinforcement learning (RL) words describe any loop where a chooser tries things and learns
from a score. The environment is the world it acts in: here the test track pairs, the renderer
and a pinned scorer version. The state is what it sees right now: a pair of tracks and their
analysis (grid, key, energy, vocals). The action is what it picks: a transition plan, meaning a
style, a mix point and the curves for each lane. The reward is the number that comes back: the
quality score M of the rendered result. The policy is the rule that maps a state to an action,
and iterating means changing the policy to earn more reward. The famous trap is reward hacking:
the policy finds what the score pays for rather than what a crowd enjoys. The defense is to
validate the score first and never change the score and the policy in the same round.

entries.one_liner: Telling the audio engine to change a gain at an exact sample, rather than as soon as it can, so a cut lands precisely on the beat.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Cuts, crossfades and sync seeks only sound tight when the change is booked at an audio time, not applied when a message arrives.
sources: Web Audio API, W3C Recommendation (AudioParam automation: setValueAtTime, linearRampToValueAtTime; render quantum of 128 frames), https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/
Wilson, A Tale of Two Clocks: Scheduling Web Audio with Precision, HTML5 Rocks / web.dev, 2013
entries.plain:
Audio is made in small blocks, 128 samples at a time in a browser (about 2.7 ms at 48 kHz).
If you tell the engine "mute this now", it can only act at the start of whichever block it is
working on when your message arrives, and you do not control which block that is. If instead you
say "mute this at sample 48,050", the engine applies it exactly there, even in the middle of a
block. That is sample-accurate scheduling: you book the change at an audio time in advance.

A hard switch at an exact sample can still click (see loop seam), so the usual move is to book a
short ramp: start at sample N, reach zero by sample N plus a few milliseconds. Booked ramps are
how cuts, kills and crossfades stay both tight and clean.
entries.in_open_dj:
The page engine books changes with Web Audio's `AudioParam` automation. The backward sync seek
blend in `apps/webui/frontend/src/lib/rb/follower-backward-blend.ts` sets a gain at a start time
and ramps it to the end time with `setValueAtTime` and `linearRampToValueAtTime`. Knob moves are
different: they use `setTargetAtTime` smoothing from the current time in
`apps/webui/frontend/src/lib/rb/audio-engine.svelte.ts`, because a knob is "now", not a beat.
The Rust engine renders in the same 128-frame quanta (`apps/audio-engine/src/stretch.rs`) and
glides parameters linearly over a fixed number of frames (`apps/audio-engine/src/dsp.rs`).

entries.one_liner: Finding where the intro, build, drop, breakdown and outro start, and snapping them to phrases of 8, 16 or 32 bars.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ snaps a model's section boundaries onto the track's own downbeats and phrase grid, and records every snap it makes.
sources: Kim and Won, All-In-One Metrical and Functional Structure Analysis with Neighborhood Attentions on Demixed Audio, WASPAA 2023, arXiv:2307.16425
Mixed In Key, Harmonic Mixing book, phrasing chapters, https://mixedinkey.com/Book/
Mueller, Fundamentals of Music Processing, Springer, 2nd ed. 2021, music structure analysis
entries.plain:
Dance music is built from blocks. Four beats make a bar, and bars come in phrases of 8, 16 or 32,
with something changing at each phrase boundary: a new element enters, the bass drops out, the
drop hits. Sections are the named blocks a DJ thinks in: intro, build, drop, breakdown, outro.
Mixing on phrase boundaries is what makes a transition feel planned rather than random, because
both tracks change at the same moment.

Section detection finds those boundaries automatically. A model listens for where the sound
changes character (energy, texture, repetition) and proposes boundary times and labels. Models
think in seconds, though, and a DJ thinks in bars, so the useful second step is to snap each
boundary onto the beat grid's downbeats and then onto a phrase multiple. A boundary that would
need a big move to snap is better left alone and flagged, because dragging it invents a phrase
the music does not have. Intros that are not a whole number of phrases (a 2-bar pickup) are why
the phrase count cannot just start at bar 1.

   snapped        *       *       *               *       *
          model lands up to a bar off  >  snapped to the phrase grid

   * = boundary   = calm   - = build   # = drop   . = breakdown
entries.in_open_dj:
`apps/analysis_structure/allin1_runner.py` runs the All-In-One model for boundaries and labels;
its beats are discarded in favor of Open DJ's own beat grid. `apps/analysis_structure/quantize.py`
snaps each boundary to a downbeat, then to a phrase multiple, keeps the raw time and the distance
moved, leaves a boundary `unsnapped` when it would move more than a bar, and votes the phrase
offset rather than assuming bar 1. `drop_events.py` and `dj_labels.py` turn sections into DJ terms.

entries.one_liner: A semitone is one piano key. Shifting a track a semitone or two can make two keys fit; more than two starts to sound processed.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Each Open DJ deck carries a key shift of -12 to +12 semitones on top of the analyzed key, which never changes.
sources: Mixed In Key, Harmonic Mixing book, https://mixedinkey.com/Book/
Zoelzer (ed.), DAFX: Digital Audio Effects, Wiley, 2nd ed. 2011, pitch shifting chapter
Wikipedia, Semitone and Pitch shift (secondary pointers)
entries.plain:
A semitone is the smallest step in Western music: one piano key to the next, white or black.
Twelve of them make an octave. In frequency terms each semitone multiplies the pitch by the
twelfth root of 2, about 1.0595, so it is a 5.9 percent change. Speed a record up 6 percent with
key lock off and it plays one semitone higher.

Pitch shifting moves a track's key without changing its tempo. It is how a DJ makes two
neighboring-but-wrong keys fit: if 8A meets 3A, shifting the second track down one semitone turns
it into 8A. The surprise is that one semitone is a big jump on the wheel: it moves seven steps,
because the wheel counts fifths. The rule is wheel steps = 7 x semitones, wrapped around 12.

Beyond about two semitones the shifter's tricks start to show. Voices change character
(chipmunk up, giant down) because their formants move with the pitch, transients smear, and
basslines can lose weight. One semitone is usually transparent, two is a judgment call, three
or more is an effect rather than a fix.

entries.one_liner: A copy of the signal is sent to an effect by a send knob, and the effect comes back on its own path while the dry track keeps playing untouched.
entries.why_it_matters_here: A send lets an echo or reverb outlive the channel it came from, which is how a DJ hides a gap or a clash at the end of a mix.
sources: Wikipedia, Aux-send, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aux-send
Udo Zoelzer (ed.), DAFX Digital Audio Effects, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2011 (parallel and serial effect structures)
entries.plain:
An insert effect is in the path: everything goes through it. A send works in parallel. A send
knob taps a copy of the channel, at whatever amount you choose, and feeds it to an effect unit.
The effect's output comes back on a return and is added to the mix. The original track never
stops being itself, and the effect has its own level and its own life. On many DJ mixers this is
the send and return jack pair on the back for outboard gear, or a send-style setting on the
built-in FX.

The key consequence: if the send is post-fader and the return is separate, closing the channel
stops new sound entering the effect but lets what is already in it ring out.

  send 0     effect hears nothing
  send 50    effect hears half
  fader down new input stops, the return keeps ringing out

entries.one_liner: An EQ that lifts or lowers everything below (low shelf) or above (high shelf) a corner frequency by the same amount.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ's LOW and HIGH knobs are shelves, so turning them all the way down makes a band much quieter but never silent.
sources: Robert Bristow-Johnson, "Audio EQ Cookbook" (lowShelf, highShelf, shelf slope S), W3C note, https://www.w3.org/TR/audio-eq-cookbook/
W3C, "Web Audio API", BiquadFilterNode types "lowshelf" and "highshelf", https://www.w3.org/TR/webaudio/
Wikipedia, "Equalization (audio)", shelving filters section (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
A shelf moves a whole end of the spectrum up or down together. A low shelf works on everything
below its corner frequency, a high shelf on everything above it, and in between there is a ramp
from the changed level back to 0 dB. Plot it and it looks like a step or a shelf, hence the name.
The bass and treble knobs on a hi-fi are shelves, and so are the low and high knobs on most DJ
mixers.

Two things to remember. First, the far end is flat: a shelf set to -26 dB turns the bass down by
26 dB and stops there. Second, the ramp is gradual, so at the corner frequency itself you get only
about half the cut in dB, and some sound just above the corner is touched too. The steepness of
that ramp is the shelf slope (called S in the cookbook formulas).

entries.one_liner: A separation score in dB: how much of a stem is the true source versus leftovers. Higher is cleaner, and turning it up or down cannot cheat.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ picks its stem models by median SI-SDR against true stems, and treats differences under 0.2 dB as inaudible.
sources: Le Roux, Wisdom, Erdogan and Hershey, SDR - half-baked or well done?, ICASSP 2019
Vincent, Gribonval and Fevotte, Performance measurement in blind audio source separation, IEEE TASLP, 2006
Rafii et al., MUSDB18, a corpus for music separation, 2017
entries.plain:
To grade a separated vocal you need the real vocal to compare against, so SI-SDR is measured on
datasets like MUSDB18 where the true stems exist. The idea is simple: split the estimate into
the part that is the real source and the part that is not (bleed, artifacts, missing bits), then
report how much louder the first part is than the second, in decibels.

"Scale-invariant" means the score finds the best volume match first, so a stem that is right but
6 dB too quiet is not punished, and a model cannot win by turning its output up. The formula is
the point here:

    target = (dot(estimate, reference) / dot(reference, reference)) * reference
    SI-SDR = 10 * log10( |target|^2 / |estimate - target|^2 )

As a feel for the scale: 0 dB means the leftovers are as loud as the source; 10 dB means they are
ten times weaker in energy. Strong current models land around 9 to 10 dB on vocals. SI-SDR does
not fully match listening: a model can win on the median and lose a blind test, so it is one
signal, not the verdict.

* estimate

   SI-SDR = 10 log10 of  target energy  over  error energy

      6 dB    error a quarter of the energy

entries.one_liner: With slip on, the track keeps playing silently underneath a loop, scratch or reverse, so letting go drops you back exactly where it would have been.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Slip lets a DJ loop, scratch or roll on a synced deck without losing the phrase, which is what makes rolls usable mid-mix.
sources: Pioneer DJ CDJ-3000 Operating Instructions (Slip mode), AlphaTheta
Serato DJ Pro Software Manual (Slip mode), Serato
entries.plain:
Normally, if you loop one beat four times and let go, the track carries on from the end of the
loop. The song is now four beats behind where it was, so it no longer lines up with the other
deck's phrases. Slip mode fixes that by keeping a hidden playhead running in the background at
normal speed. You hear the loop (or the scratch, the reverse, the brake), but the song carries on
underneath, unheard. When you release, playback jumps to the hidden playhead and you land back
in the song exactly in time, as if the trick had been played over the top.

Precisely: slip keeps a second, linear transport position that advances with the deck's tempo
whatever the audible playhead does, and on release the audible playhead seeks to it.

entries.one_liner: Rearranging a playlist so each next track is close in tempo and key to the one before, in one tap.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Most bad transitions are bad pairs; a good order removes the clashes before any mixing starts.
sources: Spotify Newsroom, Smart Reorder, Wed 25 Feb 2026, https://newsroom.spotify.com/2026-02-25/smart-reorder-playlist-mixing/
Bittner et al., Automatic Playlist Sequencing and Transitions, ISMIR 2017, https://archives.ismir.net/ismir2017/paper/000086.pdf
entries.plain:
Spotify's Smart Reorder, added to Mix on Wed 25 Feb 2026, takes a mixed playlist and reorders it
"with BPM and key", in Spotify's words. Each pair then sits closer together, so beatmatching
stretches less and the keys clash less. DJs do the same by hand when they build a set, often
with the Camelot wheel and an eye on energy.

The precise problem is ordering: find the sequence whose track-to-track costs add up smallest,
a cousin of the traveling salesman problem. Trying every order is impossible past a dozen
tracks, so solvers search cleverly. A beam search builds the set left to right and keeps only
the best few partial orders at each step.

  beam search, keep the best 3 at each step
  step 1   4A    8A    9A
  step 2   4A>9A    8A>8B    9A>8A          others dropped
  step 3   4A>9A>8A    9A>8A>8B    ...
entries.in_open_dj:
The PLAY IT solver in `apps/dj_copilot/solver.py` is a deterministic greedy beam search. It
scores each next track on key 0.35, BPM 0.35, energy 0.25 and artist repeat 0.05, follows a set
energy goal, and honors pinned opener, peak and closer tracks. It is served at
`POST /api/v1/play-it/{playlist_id}/solve` (`apps/webui/server/routes/play_it.py`). Unlike
Smart Reorder it also weighs energy, and it reports which constraints it could not meet.

entries.one_liner: A neural network unbakes a finished track into vocals, drums, bass and other. Good enough to mix with, never perfectly clean.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ renders stems with demucs models at several quality tiers and builds vocal and structure analysis on top of them.
sources: Defossez et al., Music Source Separation in the Waveform Domain, arXiv:1911.13254, 2019
Defossez, Hybrid Spectrogram and Waveform Source Separation, arXiv:2111.03600, 2021
Rouard, Massa and Defossez, Hybrid Transformers for Music Source Separation, ICASSP 2023, arXiv:2211.08553
Rafii et al., MUSDB18, a corpus for music separation, 2017
entries.plain:
A mastered track is like a baked cake: the vocals, drums, bass and synths are mixed into one
waveform. Source separation tries to unbake it. Demucs, the open model most DJ tools use, was
trained on songs whose isolated multitracks are known (the MUSDB18 dataset), so it learned what
a voice, a kick or a bassline looks like in both the waveform and the spectrogram. Give it a new
track and it predicts four stems: vocals, drums, bass and "other" (everything else). The hybrid
transformer version, htdemucs, reads both views at once and is the current common default.

Separation is a guess, so it leaves fingerprints. Bleed is the most familiar: hi-hats ghosting
into the vocal stem, a sung note leaking into "other". Artifacts are the second: a watery or
phasey sound where the model was unsure, and reverb tails chopped off. The four stems summed
come close to the original but not exactly. Heavy mixes, distorted vocals and dense synths
separate worst; clean, sparse productions separate best.

entries.one_liner: Handing one part, such as the drums, bass or vocals, from one deck to the other during a transition while the rest keeps playing.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Stems let a blend avoid two vocals or two basslines meeting, which EQ alone cannot separate cleanly.
sources: Algoriddim, djay Pro manual, Neural Mix, https://help.algoriddim.com/
Wikipedia, Music source separation, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_source_separation
entries.plain:
Source separation splits a track into stems: usually vocals, drums, bass and everything else.
With stems on both decks you can swap one part at a time. Bring B's drums in under A's vocal,
swap the bass on a downbeat, then let A's vocal finish before B's starts. An EQ bass swap does
roughly the same with frequency bands; a stem swap does it with the actual instrument, so a kick
and a bassline in the same low band can be moved separately.

The catch is quality. Separated stems carry artifacts, and a swap that is near-instant needs both
decks' stems lined up to the sample, or you hear a flam.

entries.one_liner: The libraries that do time-stretching differ in method, sound, CPU cost, latency and license; picking one is a trade, not a ranking.
entries.why_it_matters_here: The engine sets how key lock sounds, how late a synced deck can be scheduled, and what license the app can ship under.
sources: Rubber Band Library documentation (R2 Faster and R3 Finer engines, licensing), Breakfast Quay, https://breakfastquay.com/rubberband/
Mixxx 2.5 manual, Sound Hardware preferences (Keylock/Pitch-Bending Engine selector), https://manual.mixxx.org/2.5/en/chapters/preferences/sound_hardware.html
SoundTouch Audio Processing Library documentation, Olli Parviainen, https://www.surina.net/soundtouch/
Signalsmith Stretch, README and design notes, Signalsmith Audio, https://github.com/Signalsmith-Audio/signalsmith-stretch
Verhelst and Roelands, An Overlap-Add Technique Based on Waveform Similarity (WSOLA), ICASSP 1993
entries.plain:
Every time-stretcher answers the same question, "how do I make this longer or shorter without
changing its pitch?", with a different recipe, and each recipe costs something different.
SoundTouch works in the time domain: it finds where overlapping slices of waveform match best
and splices them. It is light on CPU and fine on speech and gentle changes, but grainier on dense
music. Rubber Band uses a phase vocoder. Its R2 engine (documented as "Faster") was the long
standing default; its R3 engine ("Finer", from version 3) analyzes at several resolutions at
once, which keeps both bass and transients cleaner but costs clearly more CPU. Signalsmith Stretch
is a newer phase vocoder designed for real time use with a small, MIT licensed codebase.

R3 is Rubber Band's finer engine, added in version 3; R2 is the older one. "Multithreaded Rubber
Band", as in Mixxx notes, means the stretcher's per-channel work is spread over more than one CPU
thread, so the heavier R3 engine can still keep up in real time.

License is part of the choice: SoundTouch is LGPL 2.1, Rubber Band is GPL or a paid commercial
license, Signalsmith Stretch is MIT, which is why Open DJ uses it rather than Rubber Band.

entries.one_liner: Two tracks at full gain add up, about +3 LU louder than either for different material and up to +6 dB where their peaks line up.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Any blend with both faders up gets louder in the overlap, so an auto-transition has to pull one side down or the seam jumps out.
sources: ITU-R BS.1770-5 (2023), summation of channel power in loudness measurement
Julius O. Smith III, Mathematics of the Discrete Fourier Transform, CCRMA Stanford (online book), power of sums of uncorrelated signals
EBU Tech 3341, Loudness Metering
entries.plain:
When two decks play at once, their signals add. How much louder the sum gets depends on how
alike the two signals are.

- Different tracks are uncorrelated: their waves rise and fall independently. Their powers add,
  so two equally loud tracks make a sum twice the power, +3 dB, which reads +3 LU on a loudness
  meter.
- Identical or phase-aligned material is correlated: a kick landing on both decks at the same
  instant. Their amplitudes add, so the peak doubles, +6 dB, which also eats 6 dB of headroom.

Real blends sit between the two: the beat-matched kicks are close to correlated, the pads and
vocals mostly not. That is why a long blend with both faders open feels like it surges, and why
DJs ride a fader down, swap the bass, or use an equal-power crossfader through the overlap.

uncorrelated: 10 * log10(2) = +3.01 dB    correlated: 20 * log10(2) = +6.02 dB

blends. No code measures the bump yet. It is a known trap for automatic transitions, and a proposed
rendered-transition scorer (not yet on main) is where a per-bar check would live.

entries.one_liner: The rule that turns a knob's position into a value; audio taper makes equal turns sound like equal steps, linear taper does not.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ chose a separate law for each knob (EQ linear in dB, filter even in octaves, trim linear in gain), and those choices shape how a mix feels.
sources: Rod Elliott, "Beginners' Guide to Potentiometers", Elliott Sound Products, https://sound-au.com/pots.htm
Wikipedia, "Potentiometer", audio taper section (secondary pointer)
Open DJ, (private path), Thu 20 Aug 2026
entries.plain:
A knob only reports where it is, say 0 to 100 percent. The taper law decides what that position
means. With a linear taper, halfway is half the value. With an audio taper (also called log taper,
or an "A" pot), halfway is only around a tenth to a fifth of the amplitude, roughly -14 to -20 dB.

Audio taper exists because hearing is roughly logarithmic: we judge loudness in ratios, so equal
turns should give equal steps in dB, not equal steps in amplitude. A linear volume knob does
almost everything in the first quarter of its travel and very little after that.

The same idea applies to frequency. A filter knob that moved its cutoff in equal hertz would
spend most of its turn above 10 kHz, where little seems to happen, then rush through the bass. A
law that is even in octaves (exponential in Hz) makes every part of the turn feel the same.

entries.one_liner: Moving the tempo smoothly from one track's BPM to the next over several bars of a mix, instead of jumping in one step.
entries.why_it_matters_here: An automatic transition between tracks at different tempos needs a glide, or the crowd hears a lurch at the handoff.
sources: Broughton and Brewster, How to DJ Right: The Art and Science of Playing Records, Grove Press, 2003 (riding the pitch through a mix)
Pioneer DJ CDJ-3000 Operating Instructions (Tempo range, Beat Sync), AlphaTheta
entries.plain:
Mixing a 128 BPM track into a 124 BPM one, a DJ has two choices. Jump: snap the tempo to 124 the
moment the new track takes over, a sudden 3 percent drop the room feels as a stumble. Glide:
while both tracks play, ride the pitch fader slowly, a fraction of a percent per bar, so by the
end of the blend everything sits at 124 and nobody noticed. Good DJs glide by hand; software can
do it exactly.

Precisely, a glide is a tempo curve over the transition, usually linear in BPM or in log tempo
over a whole number of bars, with both decks kept phase locked the whole way. With key lock off,
the pitch slides too (about 17 cents per percent), which is part of why glides stay small.

tempo changes, followers re-anchor through a short ramp (measured near 850 ms, recorded in

parameter glide over a fixed number of frames (`apps/audio-engine/src/dsp.rs`). A tempo glide
across a mix would belong in the auto-play handoff (`apps/webui/frontend/src/lib/rb/auto-play-handoff.ts`)
(a tempo glide is not yet in Open DJ).

entries.one_liner: Timbre is why a piano and a synth playing the same note sound different. MFCCs are the dozen numbers machines use to fingerprint it.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ does not compute MFCCs yet; a timbre feature would let track suggestions match sound, not just key and tempo.
sources: Davis and Mermelstein, Comparison of parametric representations for monosyllabic word recognition, IEEE TASSP, 1980
Mueller, Fundamentals of Music Processing, Springer, 2nd ed. 2021
Wikipedia, Mel-frequency cepstrum and Timbre (secondary pointers)
entries.plain:
Timbre is everything about a sound that is not its pitch, loudness or length: the rasp of a
saw synth, the round thud of an 808, the breath in a voice. To a machine, most of it lives in the
spectral envelope, the overall shape of which frequencies are loud, plus how that shape moves
over a note's life.

MFCCs (mel-frequency cepstral coefficients) are the classic way to boil that shape down. Take a
short slice of audio, measure its spectrum, group the frequencies into bands spaced the way the
ear hears them (the mel scale), take the log of each band's energy, then summarize the curve with
a cosine transform and keep the first dozen or so numbers. The low coefficients describe the broad
tilt and bumps; the fine detail of individual harmonics, which carries pitch, is mostly thrown
away. That makes MFCCs a good "what does this sound like" fingerprint for genre, instrument or
similarity work, and a poor one for key, which chroma handles.

   +--------------------> freq         +--------------------> freq
     808 kick  dark and low              saw lead  bright and wide

   MFCC 1-3 capture the tilt and the big bumps   =  timbre
   fine harmonic comb discarded                  =  no pitch

entries.one_liner: Changing how fast a track plays without changing its pitch, by cutting it into tiny overlapping slices and re-spacing them.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Key lock, sync at matched key and key shift all run through a stretcher, which adds latency, CPU and some artifacts.
sources: Zolzer (ed.), DAFX: Digital Audio Effects, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2011 (time-segment processing, phase vocoder)
Laroche and Dolson, Improved Phase Vocoder Time-Scale Modification of Audio, IEEE Trans. Speech and Audio Processing, 1999
Audio time stretching and pitch scaling, Wikipedia (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
Speed up a record and it goes up in pitch too, because the waves themselves get shorter. A time
stretcher breaks that link. It chops the sound into tiny overlapping slices (grains, tens of
milliseconds long), keeps each slice's pitch, and lays them back down slightly closer together
(faster) or further apart (slower). The trick is joining them without hearing the joins: a phase
vocoder works in the frequency domain and keeps each partial's phase continuous, while time
domain methods search for the best place to overlap.

It is not free. The stretcher must see a window of audio before it can output anything, which
is latency. It costs CPU on every deck. And it leaves artifacts: drum hits can smear, bass can
waver, and big stretches sound phasey or metallic.

entries.one_liner: Trim is the per-deck gain knob at the top of a channel; matching sets the incoming track's trim so it arrives as loud as the one playing.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ measures each track's LUFS, so the trim needed to match two tracks is a subtraction, not guesswork by ear.
sources: Pioneer DJ DJM-900NXS2 operating instructions, TRIM control and channel level indicator
rekordbox Operating Instructions (AlphaTheta), Auto Gain preference
entries.plain:
Trim (also called gain) sits above the EQ on every mixer channel. It sets how hot the track
enters the channel before the EQ and the volume fader touch it. Its job is to make tracks
comparable, so the fader can be used for mixing rather than for fixing level.

Loudness matching is the classic move before a blend: bring the incoming track's trim to where
it feels as loud as the outgoing one, usually by watching both channel meters while listening
in headphones. With measured loudness the arithmetic is direct. Trim in dB equals the outgoing
track's LUFS minus the incoming track's LUFS:

trim_dB = LUFS_out - LUFS_in

So a -7 LUFS incoming track against a -10 LUFS outgoing track needs -3 dB. Matching by
integrated loudness is a starting point; a quiet intro or a loud drop can still call for a
touch by ear.

entries.one_liner: True peak is the highest point of the rebuilt analog wave, which can sit above every stored sample; -1 dBTP leaves room for that overshoot.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ's loudness scan clamps any per-track gain so the gained track cannot push its true peak past -1 dBTP.
sources: ITU-R BS.1770-5 (2023), Annex 2, Guidelines for accurate measurement of true-peak level
EBU R128 (2023), Loudness normalisation and permitted maximum level of audio signals
EBU Tech 3341, Loudness Metering, EBU Mode metering to supplement EBU R128
entries.plain:
A file stores samples, dots taken tens of thousands of times a second. The sound you hear is the
smooth curve a converter draws through those dots, and that curve can swing higher between two
dots than either dot is. The sample peak only sees the dots; the true peak estimates the top of
the curve. Those hidden overs are inter-sample peaks, and they clip in a converter, a sound card
or a lossy encoder even when no stored sample reached 0 dBFS.

True peak is written in dBTP (decibels true peak). BS.1770 measures it by oversampling at least
four times at 48 kHz, which fills in points between the samples, and taking the maximum. EBU R128
sets -1 dBTP as the permitted maximum: one dB of margin for the overshoot a decoder or a
resampler adds after the master is finished.

entries.one_liner: Render several candidate transitions for one pair, show their scores, let a person pick one, and save the pick so the chooser learns.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It turns transition quality from a guess into something measured and taught by a real DJ's ear, one pick at a time.
sources: Bittner et al., Automatic Playlist Sequencing and Transitions, ISMIR 2017, https://archives.ismir.net/ismir2017/paper/000086.pdf
Bradley and Terry, Rank Analysis of Incomplete Block Designs, Biometrika, 1952
entries.plain:
For one pair of tracks there are many ways to mix: cut, filter sweep, bass swap blend, longer or
shorter, starting on this phrase or that one. A try-er renders, say, six of them offline in a
second or two, scores each on things that can be measured (beats lined up, vocals meeting,
loudness dip, key clash), and lets you audition them from the same bar so switching is seamless.
You pick one. The pick is written back as the transition for that pair, and also kept as a
lesson: this one beat those ones.

Over many picks the chooser's weights move toward your taste. The precise form is a pairwise
preference model fitted to choices, with hard vetoes kept as gates.

It would sit on the offline renderer (`odj-audio render --plan --decks-out`,

entries.one_liner: A weighted score lets strengths make up for weaknesses; a veto zeros the score on one failure, however good the rest is.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It decides whether a beautifully key-matched transition with flamming kicks can still win, which it must not.
sources: Keeney and Raiffa, Decisions with Multiple Objectives, Wiley, 1976 (additive value models)
Wikipedia, "Multiple-criteria decision analysis" (secondary pointer, compensatory versus non-compensatory methods)
entries.plain:
There are two ways to combine several checks into one score. A weighted score gives each term
some points and adds them up, so being strong on one can make up for being weak on another:
a perfect key match buys forgiveness for a small energy dip. That is a trade-off, and it suits
taste. A veto is a failure that is not negotiable. If the beats flam, or deck B lands on the
wrong downbeat, the crowd hears a mistake no matter how well the keys match, so one veto sets
the whole score to zero and names itself. In short:

    M = 0 if any veto fires, otherwise w1*x1 + w2*x2 + ...

Rule of thumb: veto what a crowd hears as an error; weight what is a matter of taste. Two traps:
too many vetoes and nothing passes, and a veto fed missing data must report "unknown", never
quietly pass.

entries.in_open_dj:
The PLAY IT ordering solver, `apps/dj_copilot/solver.py`, is purely weighted: key 0.35, BPM
0.35, energy 0.25, artist 0.05. A big key jump is recorded as a `camelot_hardcut` unmet
constraint rather than a veto, a repeated artist inside the cooldown scores 0 on its term, and a
missing key or energy scores a neutral 0.5. A proposed transition scorer (not yet on main) is the other kind: a weighted geometric mean behind vetoes for beat offset,
downbeat phase and, later, live-versus-render parity, where "unknown" never passes.

entries.one_liner: Where in a track someone is singing, measured bar by bar. Two vocals at once almost always clash, whatever the keys.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ derives vocal regions from the separated vocal stem and checks them against rekordbox's own vocal markers.
sources: Defossez, Hybrid Spectrogram and Waveform Source Separation, arXiv:2111.03600, 2021
AlphaTheta, rekordbox manual, phrase and vocal analysis sections
Wikipedia, Voice activity detection (secondary pointer)
entries.plain:
Vocal activity answers a simple question for every moment of a track: is someone singing or
rapping right now, and how strongly? The usual machine recipe is to separate the vocal stem
first, measure its loudness in short hops, compare that to the full mix or a fixed floor, and
call the stretches above threshold vocal regions. Rounded to bars, that gives a DJ a map: bars
1 to 16 instrumental, 17 to 32 verse, and so on. "Vocalness" is the continuous version, a 0 to
1 score per bar instead of a yes or no.

Two vocals at once clash for reasons beyond key. The ear follows words, and two sets of words
fight for the same attention, so both become hard to understand. Their melodies rarely share a
key or rhythm, and they sit in the same frequency band, so EQ cannot pull them apart. That is why
DJs plan blends so one vocal ends before the next starts, or run an acapella over an instrumental
on purpose.
entries.in_open_dj:
`apps/vocals/envelope.py` stores per-hop `vocals_rms` and `mix_rms` beside the vocal cache, since
vocal regions are a pure function of them. `apps/parity/vocal.py` scores rekordbox's vocal regions
against Open DJ's demucs-derived ones by overlap on a 10 Hz grid. Using vocal overlap to steer

entries.one_liner: The knob that blends the untouched track (dry) with the effect's output (wet), from no effect at all to effect only.
entries.why_it_matters_here: It is how every effect in a transition fades in and out without a jump, and Open DJ's color filter already works this way inside.
sources: Udo Zoelzer (ed.), DAFX Digital Audio Effects, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2011
AlphaTheta, DJM-900NXS2 Operating Instructions (Beat FX LEVEL/DEPTH), https://www.pioneerdj.com/
entries.plain:
Dry is the track as it is. Wet is what comes out of the effect. The mix knob decides how much of
each you hear. Fully dry, the effect is bypassed in sound even if it is running. Fully wet, you
hear only the effect, which for an echo means only repeats. Most DJ effects live somewhere in
between, and riding this knob is half of playing an effect well.

On a hardware mixer the same control is often labeled LEVEL/DEPTH. The precise form is a
crossfade between two signals, and like any crossfade it can be linear or equal-power, which
changes whether the middle sounds quieter.
entries.in_open_dj:
The Sound Color FX filter in the Rust engine is a wet/dry blend: `FilterParams` in
`apps/audio-engine/src/mixer.rs` carries a `dry` gain and two wet gains, one for the low-pass
side and one for the high-pass side. At center the knob is fully dry; turning it fades the dry
path out and the selected filter in. The planned beat FX rack (delay, echo, reverb) will need the
same control, and transition plans would ramp it like any other knob.

entries.one_liner: Running a filter forward and then backward over a whole file so its time shifts cancel; perfect for analysis, impossible during live playback.
entries.why_it_matters_here: Open DJ's offline benchmarks use it to measure stems without timing smear, while the live engine must use ordinary one-way filters.
sources: SciPy documentation, "scipy.signal.filtfilt" and "scipy.signal.sosfiltfilt", https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/signal.html
Fredrik Gustafsson, "Determining the initial states in forward-backward filtering", IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing 44(4), 1996
Julius O. Smith III, "Introduction to Digital Filters with Audio Applications" (forward-backward filtering), CCRMA Stanford, https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/filters/
entries.plain:
Every ordinary filter shifts some frequencies later in time (see group delay). Zero-phase filtering
cancels that shift with a trick: filter the whole signal forward, flip the result end to end,
filter it again, and flip it back. The second pass shifts everything the opposite way by exactly
the same amount, so nothing moves in time at any frequency. The level change is applied twice, so
the slope doubles.

The catch is that the backward pass needs the samples that come after the moment being computed.
With a file already on disk that is fine. During playback those samples have not happened yet, so
the only way to fake it is to wait, which turns into latency a DJ cannot accept. That is why
filtfilt, the name MATLAB and SciPy give the function, is an offline tool for analysis, stem
measurement and display, never for a live knob. The ends of the signal also need padding, or the
first and last moments come out distorted.
